- **Data variety**: real customers ask more varied and unexpected questions than a pilot set, so accuracy must be re-validated.
## Example
A pilot handling 200 chats per week may cost little; 50,000 chats per week multiplies token spend and exposes rare question types. Services such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and Amazon CloudWatch help, but the plan must be revisited before scaling.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pilot accuracy will hold automatically:** production traffic is larger and more varied than the pilot sample, so accuracy must be re-validated at scale.
- ✗ **B. Skip stakeholder communication:** a production rollout affects customers, support staff and compliance teams, so communication becomes more important, not less.
- ✓ **C. Reassess scalability, cost, monitoring and governance (correct):** full production changes volume, cost, risk and user variety, so each must be re-planned rather than assumed from the sandbox.
- ✗ **D. Reuse the pilot budget unchanged:** usage-based costs grow with volume, and production also adds monitoring, support and governance costs.

## Key idea
Scaling a pilot means re-planning capacity, cost, monitoring and governance for production conditions, not assuming sandbox results carry over.
Q000165:
## Tangible versus intangible KPIs
A KPI (key performance indicator) is a number leadership tracks to judge whether an initiative works. For AI business cases, KPIs fall into two groups:
- **Tangible (hard) KPIs** can be expressed directly in money or in countable operational units: incremental revenue, cost savings, hours saved, error rates, tickets resolved. They go straight into an ROI calculation.
- **Intangible (soft) KPIs** are real benefits that are hard to price precisely: brand perception, employee morale, customer sentiment, innovation culture. They are usually measured with surveys or indexes and reported alongside, not inside, the financial numbers.
## Example
A retailer adds AI product recommendations. Revenue from orders that include a recommended item, compared with a control group, is tangible. A survey saying customers "feel the site understands them" is intangible, even though it may eventually lead to revenue.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Incremental revenue from AI recommendations (correct):** it is money the AI system added on top of the baseline, measurable in dollars (ideally against a control group), so it enters ROI directly.
- ✓ **B. Cost savings from automating a manual process (correct):** fewer labor hours or lower processing cost is a direct, countable financial result that a leadership report can total and compare to spend.
- ✗ **C. Improved brand perception:** being seen as an innovator is valuable, but it is measured through surveys or reputation indexes and has no direct dollar value, so it is an intangible benefit.
- ✗ **D. Higher employee morale:** less repetitive work can improve retention and engagement, but morale itself is a soft outcome measured by surveys, not a hard financial result.
- ✗ **E. Better customer sentiment:** survey scores show how customers feel; they may predict future revenue but are not themselves a financial figure the report can count as ROI.

## Key idea
Hard KPIs are money or countable operational results (revenue, savings); brand, morale and sentiment are real but intangible benefits reported separately.
Q000166:
## The basic ROI formula
Return on investment compares what an initiative gains with what it costs:
`ROI = (Gain - Cost) / Cost`, usually shown as a percentage.
- Gain is the total benefit attributed to the initiative (cost savings plus new revenue).
- Cost is the total investment for the same period (build, licenses, infrastructure, people, change management).
- A negative ROI means the initiative has not yet paid back its cost in that period; it does not automatically mean the project is a failure.
## Working the numbers
Gain = 200,000 and Cost = 500,000.
`(200,000 - 500,000) / 500,000 = -300,000 / 500,000 = -0.6`, so the year-one ROI is -60 percent.
AI projects often show a negative first year because implementation costs land up front, while benefits accumulate over several years. That is why business cases also look at multi-year ROI and payback period.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 250 percent:** this is Cost divided by Gain (500,000 / 200,000 = 2.5), which inverts the ratio and ignores that the gain is smaller than the cost.
- ✓ **B. Negative 60 percent (correct):** subtracting the 500,000 cost from the 200,000 gain gives a net loss of 300,000, and dividing by the 500,000 cost gives -0.6, or -60 percent for year one.
- ✗ **C. 150 percent:** this is the net difference divided by the gain (300,000 / 200,000) and drops the negative sign, so both the denominator and the direction are wrong.
- ✗ **D. 40 percent:** this is Gain divided by Cost (200,000 / 500,000), which shows how much of the cost was recovered but not the net return after subtracting the cost.

## Key idea
Subtract the cost first, then divide by the cost: a 200,000 gain on a 500,000 investment is -60 percent ROI, not a recovery ratio like 40 percent.
Q000167:
## Leading versus lagging indicators
- A **lagging indicator** reports an outcome after it has happened: quarterly revenue, annual profit, year-end customer lifetime value. It is the final score, but it arrives too late to steer.
- A **leading indicator** moves early and predicts the outcome: adoption, engagement, conversion steps. If it drops, you can act before revenue drops.
## Example for a recommendation engine
The causal chain is roughly: users see recommendations, click them, add items, buy, and come back.
- Weekly feature usage and click-through rate sit at the start of that chain and can be read within days of launch.
- Quarterly revenue and annual CLV sit at the end and only confirm success months later.
Good AI programs track both: leading indicators to adjust the product quickly, lagging indicators to prove business value.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Conference sessions attended by the team:** this measures team activity, not user behavior or business outcomes, so it predicts nothing about the engine's success.
- ✗ **B. Quarterly total revenue growth:** revenue is the outcome itself, reported after the fact and influenced by many factors beyond the engine, which makes it a lagging indicator.
- ✗ **C. Annual customer lifetime value:** CLV reported at year-end summarizes a whole year of behavior and arrives far too late to steer the product, so it is lagging.
- ✓ **D. Weekly click-through rate on recommendations (correct):** it measures whether users find the suggestions relevant, changes within days of a model or UI change, and predicts later purchases.
- ✓ **E. Weekly active usage rate of the feature (correct):** adoption must come before any revenue impact, and a weekly usage trend gives an early signal of whether the engine will deliver.

## Key idea
Engagement signals like weekly usage and click-through move first and predict results; revenue and CLV confirm results only after the fact.
Q000168:
## Why generative AI costs follow users
Most managed generative AI services, including Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference, charge per unit of consumption, typically per input and output token. Cost therefore scales with how many requests users send and how long the prompts and answers are.
If users suddenly start pasting long documents or a feature goes viral, the bill rises the same day, regardless of the budget plan.
## Controls that tie spend to policy
- **Quotas and rate limits**: cap requests or tokens per user, team or application (for example through an API gateway usage plan or application-level throttling).
- **Budgets and alerts**: AWS Budgets can notify owners when actual or forecasted spend crosses a threshold, and Budgets actions can apply restrictive controls.
- **Design levers**: shorter prompts, response length limits, caching, and routing simple requests to smaller, cheaper models.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fixed annual seat-based license:** switching every use case to per-user pricing is often not available for API-based model consumption and can mean paying for unused seats; it changes the billing shape rather than managing the behavior driving usage.
- ✗ **B. Removing cost monitoring dashboards:** taking away visibility makes spikes harder to see and explain, so costs would stay unpredictable and be discovered even later.
- ✓ **C. Usage quotas, rate limits, or consumption budget alerts (correct):** these act on the exact driver of the problem, per-request consumption by end users, by capping it and warning owners before spikes become surprise bills.
- ✗ **D. Accepting the cost increase:** this applies no control at all and leaves spending entirely at the mercy of user behavior, which is the problem the company wants to solve.

## Key idea
When cost is driven by user consumption, control the consumption itself with quotas, rate limits and budget alerts instead of hiding or merely re-packaging the bill.
Q000169:
## Three common AI pricing models
- **Consumption-based (pay-per-use)**: you pay for each request, token, image or minute processed. Examples: Amazon Bedrock on-demand tokens, Amazon Rekognition per image, Amazon Transcribe per second of audio. Costs follow usage exactly and drop to near zero when idle.
- **Instance-based (provisioned capacity)**: you pay per hour for compute you keep running, such as a SageMaker real-time endpoint instance or an EC2 instance, whether or not it is busy.
- **Seat-based (per user)**: you pay a fixed amount per user per month for an application, for example an AI assistant subscription such as Amazon Q Business.
## Choosing between them
Spiky or unknown traffic suits consumption pricing; steady high traffic can be cheaper on provisioned instances; broad employee productivity tools are commonly priced per seat.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Consumption-based, instance-based, seat-based (correct):** per API call is paying for each unit consumed, hourly endpoint billing is paying for provisioned instance time, and per user per month is a seat license, in exactly the order listed.
- ✗ **B. All three are consumption-based:** only the per-call price varies with actual usage; an hourly instance is billed even when idle and a per-user fee is charged regardless of how much each user does.
- ✗ **C. Seat-based, consumption-based, instance-based:** this labels the per-call service as per-user pricing and the per-user assistant as instance pricing, which shifts every definition by one position.
- ✗ **D. Instance-based, seat-based, consumption-based:** this calls the per-request service an hourly instance and the per-user subscription consumption pricing, reversing what each model charges for.

## Key idea
Per request is consumption, per hour of running capacity is instance-based, per user per month is seat-based.
Q000170:
## Discount options for steady AWS compute
- **On-Demand**: no commitment, full price.
- **Savings Plans**: you commit to a consistent amount of spend per hour (for example 20 dollars per hour) for one or three years and get lower rates on usage up to that amount.
- **Compute Savings Plans** apply across EC2 instance families, sizes, Regions and operating systems, and also to AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda, but they do not cover SageMaker usage.
- **SageMaker Savings Plans** apply to eligible Amazon SageMaker usage (such as training, real-time inference and notebooks) regardless of instance family, size or Region.
- **Spot Instances**: large discounts on spare capacity, but AWS can reclaim them with a two-minute warning.
- **Dedicated Hosts**: a whole physical server for you, mainly for per-socket or per-core software licensing and compliance needs.
## Example
A company runs inference endpoints around the clock all year. A one-year SageMaker Savings Plan covers the endpoints, a Compute Savings Plan covers the EC2 side, and both still apply if the team moves to a newer instance family mid-year.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. On-Demand with no commitment:** it is flexible but charges the full rate, so it gives no discount for usage the company already knows will run all year.
- ✗ **B. Dedicated Hosts for three years:** dedicated physical servers serve licensing and compliance needs, cost more for this purpose, tie capacity to specific host types, and a three-year term exceeds the one-year plan.
- ✓ **C. A Compute or SageMaker Savings Plan (correct):** a one-year commitment matches the one-year steady workload and gives a significant discount over On-Demand; a Compute Savings Plan covers the EC2 usage and a SageMaker Savings Plan covers the SageMaker usage, and both apply across instance families so the team keeps flexibility.
- ✗ **D. Spot for always-on endpoints:** Spot capacity can be interrupted with two minutes' notice, which is unsuitable for endpoints that must serve inference continuously.

## Key idea
Steady, predictable compute for a year calls for Savings Plans, which discount committed spend while still allowing instance-family changes; Spot and Dedicated Hosts solve different problems.
Q000171:
## AWS cost tools and what each is for
- **AWS Cost Explorer** visualizes past and current AWS spend. You can group and filter by service, linked account, Region, usage type or cost allocation tags, view daily or monthly trends, and see forecasts.
- **AWS Pricing Calculator** estimates the cost of an architecture before you build it; it knows nothing about what you actually spent.
- **AWS Budgets** sets thresholds and alerts on actual or forecasted spend.
- **Cost and Usage Reports / Data Exports** deliver line-item billing data for detailed analysis in tools such as Amazon Athena or Amazon QuickSight.
## Example
Three months after launch, the finance team opens Cost Explorer, groups by service, and sees that Amazon Bedrock and a SageMaker endpoint make up most of the solution's spend. Adding a project cost allocation tag lets them isolate the AI solution from other workloads.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Cost Explorer (correct):** it analyzes historical spend with trend charts and lets the team group costs by service (and by tags), which is exactly how to find the components driving the most cost.
- ✗ **B. AWS Pricing Calculator:** it produces estimates for planned architectures from list prices and does not read the account's actual billing history.
- ✗ **C. Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics:** it runs scripted canaries that test endpoints and user journeys for availability and latency; it has nothing to do with billing data.
- ✗ **D. AWS Marketplace:** it is a catalog for buying third-party software, data and services, not a tool for analyzing an account's spending trends.

## Key idea
Historical spend analysis by service is Cost Explorer; the Pricing Calculator only estimates what something would cost before you run it.
Q000172:
## Attribution: counting only what the AI caused
ROI is only meaningful if the gain in the formula is the gain the investment actually produced. That is called **incremental** impact: the difference between what happened with the AI system and what would have happened without it.
- A business unit that earned 50 million dollars last year would have earned most of that without any AI.
- If AI recommendations lifted revenue by 1 million dollars, the gain is 1 million dollars, not 50 million.
## How teams measure incremental impact
- A/B tests or holdout groups that do not get the AI feature
- Before-and-after comparisons against a pre-AI baseline, adjusted for seasonality
- Tracking only the savings from tasks the AI actually replaced

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Never include revenue, only cost savings:** revenue gains are a legitimate part of ROI when they are incremental and attributable; excluding them would understate the value of many AI projects.
- ✗ **B. No flaw:** total business-unit revenue is not an appropriate baseline, because most of it is unrelated to the AI system, so the calculation cannot reflect the AI's real return.
- ✓ **C. It overstates ROI by counting revenue the AI didn't cause (correct):** dividing total business-unit revenue by the AI system's cost credits the AI with sales that existing products, staff and customers would have generated anyway, inflating the result enormously.
- ✗ **D. Only flaw is missing AWS costs:** a complete cost figure matters, but the problem described is on the gain side, where unrelated revenue is being counted.

## Key idea
ROI must use the incremental gain the AI caused (measured against a baseline or control), not the total revenue of the business it sits in.
Q000173:
## What a baseline is
A baseline is the measured value of a metric before a change is introduced. Improvement targets like "reduce resolution time by 30 percent" only make sense relative to that starting point.
## Example
- Before the AI assistant, the team measures average ticket resolution time over three months: 10 hours.
- A 30 percent reduction means the target is 7 hours.
- After launch, the team measures again with the same definition and time window. If the average is 8 hours, they achieved 20 percent and are not yet at target.
Good baselines use the same definitions, data sources and comparable periods as the later measurements, so the difference reflects the AI and not a change in how things were counted.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only for marketing purposes:** the baseline is a measurement tool at the core of evaluation; marketing may quote results, but they are computed from the baseline.
- ✗ **B. Set equal to the target value:** a baseline is measured, not chosen; setting it to the target would show zero change and make progress impossible to measure.
- ✗ **C. Irrelevant once the target is set:** a percentage target is relative, so it depends on the baseline throughout the project to compute actual improvement.
- ✓ **D. It's the pre-AI reference point for measuring progress (correct):** without a measured starting value there is nothing to compute a 30 percent reduction from, so the baseline is what turns the target into a checkable number.

## Key idea
A percentage improvement target is meaningless without a measured pre-AI baseline to compare against.
Q000174:
## Reporting tangible and intangible benefits
Financial ROI uses benefits that can be expressed in money: revenue, cost reductions, hours saved converted to cost. Other benefits are real but do not have a reliable price:
- employee morale and engagement
- brand reputation
- customer trust and satisfaction
- faster learning and innovation capacity
## Why report them separately
Mixing guessed dollar values for morale into ROI makes the whole number less credible to a CFO. The common practice is to show hard ROI on its own and list intangible benefits beside it, supported by indicators such as engagement survey scores or attrition trends.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Higher employee morale from less manual work (correct):** morale is a genuine benefit, but it is measured through surveys or proxies rather than dollars, so it is intangible and belongs next to, not inside, the ROI figures.
- ✗ **B. $2 million in new revenue:** a dollar amount of revenue attributed to recommendations is a direct financial result and is tangible.
- ✗ **C. 30% fewer invoice processing hours:** hours saved are counted operationally and convert directly to labor cost, so this is a tangible benefit.
- ✗ **D. 12% reduction in call handling costs:** a measured cost reduction is a hard financial figure that goes straight into ROI.

## Key idea
Anything already expressed in money or countable hours is tangible; morale is real value but intangible, so it is reported alongside ROI.
Q000175:
## Matching pricing commitments to certainty
Pricing options trade flexibility for discount:
- **On-demand / pay-as-you-go**: highest unit price, but no commitment. If the project stops, spending stops.
- **Commitments** (Savings Plans, reserved capacity, multi-year licenses): lower unit price, but you pay for the committed amount whether or not you use it, for the whole term.
A commitment only saves money if actual usage stays at or above the committed level for the full term.
## Example
A pilot might be cancelled after six months. A three-year commitment would leave roughly two and a half years of payments for something no longer in use, wiping out any discount. Paying on demand costs more per unit, but total exposure ends when the pilot ends. Once usage is steady and the project is confirmed, the company can buy commitments sized to real data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reserved capacity for year-three usage:** it commits the startup to paying for capacity sized for a future it may never reach, and the payments continue even if the pilot is stopped.
- ✗ **B. Long-term seat license for maximum users:** it locks in payment for many users who do not exist yet, for a term far longer than the six-month pilot window.
- ✗ **C. 3-year All Upfront Savings Plan:** it pays three years of committed spend in advance for a workload that may end in six months, turning the discount into a large loss.
- ✓ **D. On-demand pricing until usage patterns stabilize (correct):** it carries no commitment, so a cancelled or small pilot only costs what it actually used, and later commitments can be sized on real usage.

## Key idea
When usage is uncertain and the project may stop soon, avoid commitments and pay on demand; commit only once usage is proven and stable.
Q000176:
## Assessing the competitive landscape for AI
A competitive landscape assessment studies how competitors and new entrants are using AI, and where the market is heading, so the company can decide where AI creates an advantage for it specifically.
Typical questions:
- Which AI capabilities do competitors already offer customers, and how well do they work?
- Which customer needs are poorly served by anyone?
- What assets do we have that others lack (data, distribution, domain expertise)?
- Where is AI becoming table stakes, and where can it still differentiate?
## Example
An insurer finds that rivals already offer AI claims chat, but nobody offers instant damage estimates from photos. With years of labeled claims photos, it targets that gap.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Analyzing competitors' AI use to find gaps and edges (correct):** the assessment maps what others do and how well, so the company can invest where it can differentiate and match only where AI has become expected.
- ✗ **B. Buying the same vendors and tools as competitors:** using identical tools produces similar capabilities, which may be needed for parity but does not by itself create any differentiation.
- ✗ **C. Copying whatever features competitors launch:** pure imitation always trails the market and cannot create an edge; the assessment is meant to find where the company can lead.
- ✗ **D. Focusing only on internal efficiency projects:** this ignores competitors and customers entirely, so it cannot answer where AI differentiates the company in its market.

## Key idea
A competitive assessment studies rivals' AI to find gaps the company can own, not to copy them or look only inward.
Q000177:
## Efficiency gains versus business-model transformation
AI can create value at different levels:
- **Operational efficiency**: doing the same work faster or cheaper (predictive maintenance in the factory, automated quality inspection).
- **Product enhancement**: making the existing product better.
- **Business-model transformation**: changing how the company creates and captures value, for example new revenue streams, new customers, or moving from one-time sales to recurring services.
## The car example
Selling a car is a one-time transaction. Monitoring vehicle health through connected data, then selling personalized maintenance and insurance as a subscription, creates an ongoing relationship and recurring revenue that did not exist before. AI is what makes the personalization and prediction possible at scale.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Leading indicator of employee productivity:** a leading indicator is a metric that predicts an outcome; the scenario describes a strategic change in the business, not a measurement.
- ✓ **B. Business-model transformation (correct):** AI moves the company from one-time product sales to recurring, data-driven services with new revenue streams, which changes how it makes money, not just how efficiently it builds cars.
- ✗ **C. Cost optimization only:** the manufacturing efficiency gain is only part of the story; launching subscription maintenance and insurance products adds revenue, which cost optimization does not describe.
- ✗ **D. Build-versus-buy sourcing decision:** that decision is about how to obtain a capability (develop, purchase or partner), while the scenario is about what the company sells and how it earns revenue.

## Key idea
When AI creates new revenue streams and turns products into ongoing services, that is business-model transformation, beyond efficiency.
Q000178:
## The data flywheel
A data flywheel is a self-reinforcing loop:
1. More customers use the product.
2. Their interactions generate proprietary data (clicks, purchases, feedback).
3. That data improves the model.
4. Better recommendations attract and retain more customers, and the loop repeats.
## Why it is hard to copy
A competitor can use the same algorithms or foundation models, but it cannot download your users' behavior history. Every month the loop runs, the gap in data and model quality can grow. This is why proprietary data is often described as a moat, while features built only on public models are easy to match.
The advantage still needs maintenance: data quality, privacy compliance and continued model improvement keep the flywheel turning.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Temporary first-mover advantage:** being first alone erodes once others launch, but here the advantage compounds with continued usage and proprietary data, which makes it durable.
- ✗ **B. Seat-based pricing structure:** seat pricing describes how customers are charged per user and says nothing about why the engine improves or is hard to copy.
- ✓ **C. An advantage from a hard-to-copy proprietary data flywheel (correct):** usage creates unique data, the data improves the engine, and the better engine drives more usage, a loop competitors cannot replicate without the same users and history.
- ✗ **D. Build-buy-partner sourcing decision:** that is about how to acquire the capability, whereas the scenario explains why the resulting capability stays ahead of competitors.

## Key idea
Proprietary data that grows with usage and keeps improving the model is a durable advantage; being first or picking a pricing model is not.
Q000179:
## Sizing AI investment
Both extremes are risky:
- **Overinvesting**: large budgets committed before any use case has shown value, spread across too many projects, or on infrastructure no one uses yet.
- **Underinvesting**: waiting until the market is fully proven, which lets competitors build data, skills and customer expectations first.
## The incremental approach
1. Pick a few use cases tied to measurable business value (cost, revenue, risk).
2. Run small pilots with clear success criteria and baselines.
3. Scale the ones that meet their targets, stop the ones that do not, and reinvest the lessons.
Managed and pay-as-you-go services, such as Amazon Bedrock, help keep early costs proportional to use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Avoid AI until competitors prove the market:** removing all risk means entering late, after rivals have built data advantages and customer expectations have moved on, which is underinvestment.
- ✗ **B. Maximum budget immediately regardless of use cases:** spending before value is proven risks large losses the limited capital cannot absorb, which is overinvestment.
- ✗ **C. Equal investment across every possible use case:** spreading scarce funds evenly starves the most valuable projects and funds weak ones, so none gets enough to succeed.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Scale investment incrementally, starting with value-tied pilots: limited capital goes first to use cases with measurable value, results decide what gets more funding, and the company builds capability without betting everything up front.

## Key idea
With limited capital, fund a few value-tied pilots and scale what works, avoiding both all-in bets and waiting on the sidelines.
Q000180:
## From product sales to a platform model
- A **product (transactional) model** sells discrete items: each e-book is a one-time sale, and the relationship ends at checkout.
- A **platform or service model** gives customers ongoing access to a system that creates value continuously: personalized bundles on demand, recommendations that learn from each use, and pricing tied to usage or subscription.
## What AI changes here
Generative AI lets the publisher produce personalized content bundles for each customer at a cost that would be impossible manually, and recommendation models keep curating as preferences evolve. Revenue shifts from counting units sold to recurring usage-based subscriptions, and the customer relationship becomes continuous. That is a change in the revenue model and value proposition, not just a process tweak.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Purely internal cost reduction:** the change is customer-facing (personalized bundles, new subscription) and alters pricing, so it is not an internal efficiency project.
- ✗ **B. Build-buy-partner sourcing decision:** sourcing is about how the publisher obtains its AI technology; the scenario describes what it sells and how customers pay.
- ✗ **C. Minor operational efficiency with no revenue change:** the revenue model changes explicitly from per-title sales to usage-based subscription, which is the opposite of no change.
- ✓ **D. A shift from product sales to an AI-driven platform model (correct):** the company moves from selling individual e-books to an ongoing, personalized, usage-based subscription service that AI makes possible, which transforms how it earns revenue.

## Key idea
When AI turns one-time product sales into a continuous, personalized subscription service, the business model itself has been transformed.
Q000181:
## Temporary versus sustainable AI advantages
An advantage is sustainable when competitors cannot easily obtain it, even with money and time.
- **Easy to copy**: anything built on the same public foundation models, being first to announce something, marketing campaigns, features that are simple prompt layers.
- **Hard to copy**: proprietary data that keeps growing, models tuned on that data, AI embedded deeply into workflows and systems that customers depend on, and organizational skills built over years.
## Example
Two banks use the same foundation model. One also grounds it in fifteen years of its own customer interaction data and embeds it into underwriting, service and fraud workflows. A rival can license the same model tomorrow but cannot recreate the data or the integration quickly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Same public foundation model as everyone:** any competitor can access the identical model, so it offers parity, not differentiation.
- ✗ **B. First to announce a chatbot pilot:** an announcement gives brief attention, and competitors can launch their own chatbots quickly, so the edge fades.
- ✗ **C. Short-term marketing campaign:** a campaign ends and can be matched by rivals; it creates awareness, not a capability others cannot build.
- ✓ **D. Proprietary, improving data and deeply integrated workflows (correct):** unique data that grows over time and AI woven into core processes take competitors years to replicate, so the edge lasts.

## Key idea
Advantages that last come from assets rivals cannot get, like proprietary data and deep workflow integration, not from shared models or announcements.
Q000182:
## Concentration risk in AI investments
Putting almost all of a budget into one unproven initiative concentrates risk:
- **Failure exposure**: if the initiative fails, most of the year's technology investment produces little value.
- **Lost flexibility**: little money is left to fund other opportunities, react to market changes, or fix problems the initiative uncovers.
- **Opportunity cost**: other projects, including basic maintenance and security work, may be starved.
## The usual mitigation
Pilot first, set measurable gates, and fund in stages. A portfolio of smaller bets with clear success criteria lets the company scale the winners and stop the losers early.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Concentration raises failure exposure and cuts flexibility (correct):** one untested bet on nearly the whole budget means a failure wastes most of the investment and leaves no capacity to pursue alternatives or adapt.
- ✗ **B. Larger investments always return proportionally more:** returns depend on whether the use case works, and an unpiloted initiative has no evidence it will; size alone does not guarantee returns.
- ✗ **C. AWS pricing eliminates financial risk:** pay-as-you-go pricing can reduce infrastructure commitments, but it cannot make an unproven business initiative succeed or recover budget spent on staff, change and licenses.
- ✗ **D. Purely technical risk:** the main danger is strategic and financial (budget concentration, opportunity cost), not just whether the technology functions.

## Key idea
Committing the whole budget to one unproven AI initiative concentrates failure risk and removes flexibility; pilot and fund in stages instead.
Q000183:
## Competitive timing strategies
- **First mover**: launches a new capability before anyone else. Possible upside: learning early, capturing customers and data first. Downside: pays for experiments, market education and mistakes.
- **Fast follower**: lets others test the market, watches what works, then adopts quickly and improves on it. Upside: lower risk and cost, benefits from others' lessons. Downside: may face entrenched leaders if it moves too slowly.
- **Late adopter**: waits until the technology is mature and standard.
## Example
A retailer waits until rivals show that AI shopping assistants raise conversion, then launches its own within months, with better integration into its loyalty program.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. First-mover strategy:** a first mover goes first to pioneer the use case, which is the opposite of letting competitors lead.
- ✗ **B. Build-buy-partner sourcing decision:** that is about how to acquire an AI capability, not when to enter the market relative to competitors.
- ✗ **C. Guaranteed sustainable competitive advantage:** no timing strategy guarantees a lasting advantage, and following others often yields parity unless the improvements are hard to copy.
- ✓ **D. Fast-follower strategy (correct):** the company intentionally lets competitors take the pioneering risk, then quickly adopts and improves validated approaches, which is the definition of a fast follower.

## Key idea
Letting others pioneer and then quickly adopting and improving is fast following, not first moving.
Q000184:
## Disruption through AI-enabled business models
Disruption often does not come from doing the old business slightly better; it comes from a new model that changes customer expectations.
In ride-hailing, AI and data enabled:
- matching riders and drivers in real time
- dynamic pricing that balances supply and demand
- predicting demand to position drivers
Customers came to expect booking through an app, visible arrival times and upfront prices, and companies relying on phone dispatch lost share.
## Lesson
Leaders should ask not only "can AI make our process cheaper?" but "could a competitor use AI to redefine how customers get what we sell?" Treating such shifts as a passing trend is a classic strategic blind spot.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Correctly avoided unnecessary AI investment:** the outcome shows the investment was necessary; competitors using AI captured most of the market.
- ✗ **B. Invested too heavily in AI too early:** the company made no changes and no investment at all, so over-investment cannot be its error.
- ✗ **C. Should have pursued legal action:** competitors using AI to match rides and set prices is normal competition; lawsuits would not address the company's lack of an adapted business model.
- ✓ **D. It missed that AI could transform its business model (correct):** competitors used AI to change how the service is delivered and priced, and by dismissing that shift the company failed to adapt its own model and lost the market.

## Key idea
The error was dismissing an AI-enabled business model shift as a fad; disruption comes from new models, not just new tools.
Q000185:
## Data network effects
A **network effect** means a product becomes more valuable as more people use it. A marketplace already has one: more sellers attract more buyers and vice versa.
A **data network effect** adds a second loop: every search, click and transaction becomes training data that improves the matching algorithm, so each new user also makes matches better for everyone else.
## Why it becomes a moat
- A newcomer starts with few users and little data, so its matches are worse, which makes it harder to attract users.
- The leader's advantage grows with scale rather than shrinking.
- The algorithm itself can often be reproduced; the accumulated users and interaction data cannot.
The advantage still needs ongoing investment in data quality, model updates and trust to keep compounding.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Value compounds with adoption; scale and data are hard to copy: each additional buyer and seller improves matching for all users, and competitors cannot replicate the accumulated user base and interaction data even if they write a similar algorithm.
- ✗ **B. Competitors can't legally use similar algorithms:** matching algorithms are widely known and generally not legally exclusive; the advantage comes from users and data, not legal barriers.
- ✗ **C. Needs no further investment once launched:** the model must keep being retrained, monitored and improved, and the platform must keep earning trust, or the advantage erodes.
- ✗ **D. Code is secret and can't be reverse-engineered:** similar algorithms can be built independently from public research; secrecy of the code is not what makes the advantage durable.

## Key idea
Durability comes from compounding users and data (data network effects), not from secret or legally protected algorithms.
Q000186:
## Responsible AI dimensions
Common responsible AI dimensions include fairness, explainability, privacy and security, **safety**, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance and transparency.
- **Safety** means preventing the system from producing harmful output or causing harm, which is critical in health, finance and other high-stakes domains.
## Mitigations for unsafe outputs
- **Guardrails**: for example, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can block denied topics, filter harmful content, and use contextual grounding checks to flag answers that are not supported by the supplied reference content.
- **Testing**: red-teaming and evaluation sets with dangerous edge cases, such as dosage questions, before and after launch.
- **Scope limits**: restrict the bot to general information and refuse individualized dosing advice.
- **Human escalation**: route risky questions to pharmacists or clinicians.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Controllability; let users change model settings:** controllability is about operators being able to steer and monitor system behavior, and letting end users tweak settings would not stop dangerous dosage answers.
- ✗ **B. Privacy; encrypt conversation logs:** encryption protects stored data from exposure, but it does nothing to prevent the model from generating unsafe medical advice.
- ✗ **C. Fairness; balance user demographics:** fairness concerns equitable outcomes across groups; the problem here is harmful content for any user, not unequal treatment.
- ✓ **D. Safety; add guardrails, testing, and human escalation (correct):** recommending unsafe doses is harmful output, which is a safety failure, and layered guardrails, adversarial testing and handoff to qualified humans reduce that harm.

## Key idea
Harmful output such as unsafe medical advice is a safety failure, addressed with guardrails, testing and human escalation rather than privacy or fairness controls.
Q000187:
## Responsible AI by design
Responsible AI practices are most effective and cheapest when they shape the system from the start, the same idea as security by design.
At the design stage, the team can:
- define intended use, users and out-of-scope uses
- run a risk and impact assessment (who could be harmed, how badly)
- choose data sources and check them for bias and consent
- set fairness, safety and quality metrics and acceptance thresholds
- plan guardrails, human oversight and monitoring
These practices then continue through development, testing, launch and operation.
## Why not later
Discovering bias after the feature is built can mean new data, retraining or redesign. Discovering it after launch adds harm to users, reputational damage and possible regulatory exposure.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only after a customer complaint:** waiting for complaints means harm has already reached users, and fixing it then is slower, costlier and damages trust.
- ✓ **B. During initial design, before development begins (correct):** early risk assessment and bias planning shape data, model and product choices when changes are cheapest and before anyone can be harmed.
- ✗ **C. Only after the feature is fully built:** issues found at that stage often require redesign or new data, and fixed design choices limit which mitigations are still possible.
- ✗ **D. Only when a regulator requests an audit:** this is purely reactive and treats responsible AI as compliance paperwork rather than a way to prevent harm.

## Key idea
Integrate responsible AI at design time and keep it through the lifecycle, rather than reacting to complaints, launches or audits.
Q000188:
## Speed versus risk in generative AI launches
Launch decisions often trade time-to-market against risk reduction.
- **Red-teaming**: deliberately trying to make the chatbot misbehave (jailbreaks, harmful content, leaking data, false claims).
- **Bias evaluation**: testing whether answers differ unfairly across groups.
Skipping or shortening these steps gets the product out sooner but raises the chance of a public failure: offensive answers, wrong commitments to customers, or data exposure, each carrying reputational, legal and financial costs.
## Framing the decision
Leaders weigh the value of launching six weeks earlier against the expected cost of an incident. Options include a limited or staged launch, stricter guardrails for the initial release, or launching internally first while testing continues.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cloud versus on-premises deployment:** the disagreement is about testing time before launch, not about where the chatbot is hosted.
- ✗ **B. Model accuracy versus training cost:** nobody is proposing to spend more on training; the extra weeks are for safety and bias evaluation of the deployed system.
- ✗ **C. Data privacy versus data residency:** neither where data is stored nor privacy controls is the subject of the dispute; it is launch timing against testing depth.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Time-to-market speed versus reduced risk exposure and reputational protection: the four-week launch captures competitive advantage sooner, while the extra six weeks of red-teaming and bias checks lower the chance of harmful or embarrassing failures.

## Key idea
Launching fast versus testing thoroughly is a time-to-market versus risk-exposure tradeoff, and responsible AI testing is how the risk side is reduced.
Q000189:
## Human oversight and decision stakes
The amount of human oversight should rise with the potential impact of an AI decision on people.
- **Low stakes**: product recommendations, email sorting. Full automation is usually acceptable, with monitoring.
- **High stakes**: hiring, termination, credit, insurance, healthcare, legal outcomes. Errors can seriously harm individuals, and many regulations and ethics frameworks expect meaningful human review and a way to contest the outcome.
## Patterns
- **Human-in-the-loop**: a person reviews and approves before the decision takes effect.
- **Human-on-the-loop**: a person monitors and can intervene.
AWS offers Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) to route selected predictions to human reviewers, for example low-confidence or high-impact cases.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only customer decisions, not employees:** employees are affected just as seriously by AI decisions, and employment decisions are widely treated as high-stakes.
- ✗ **B. Never, if the model was tested before launch:** pre-launch testing cannot catch every individual error or drift over time, and it does not provide accountability for decisions about specific people.
- ✗ **C. Only below 50% accuracy:** even a highly accurate model makes errors, and in termination decisions each error harms a real person, so oversight is needed regardless of an accuracy threshold.
- ✓ **D. High-stakes decisions affecting people (correct):** terminating employment seriously affects someone's livelihood, so a human must review the AI's recommendation, check context the model may miss, and remain accountable.

## Key idea
The higher the impact on people, the more human oversight is needed; accuracy or pre-launch testing does not replace review of high-stakes decisions.
Q000190:
## Transparency and model documentation
**Transparency** in responsible AI means giving stakeholders enough information to understand what a system is, how it was built, what it is for, and where it can fail.
A **model card** is a standard document that records:
- intended use cases and out-of-scope uses
- training data sources at a suitable level of detail
- evaluation results and known limitations or risks
AWS supports this with Amazon SageMaker Model Cards for documenting your own models, and publishes AWS AI Service Cards for some of its own AI services.
## Why it matters
Customers, auditors and regulators use this information to decide whether a model fits their use, to spot risks early, and to hold providers accountable. Withholding it makes users rely on the system blindly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reduced robustness against adversarial attacks:** robustness depends on how the model is built and defended, not on whether its documentation is public, so hiding a model card does not directly weaken it.
- ✗ **B. Lower costs with no offsetting risk:** skipping publication may save a little effort, but it carries the risk of lost trust and harder accountability, so it is not risk-free.
- ✓ **C. Reduced transparency, which can erode trust (correct):** without information on data sources, limitations and intended use, stakeholders cannot judge whether the model is appropriate, which weakens trust and accountability.
- ✗ **D. Improved fairness across groups:** withholding documentation does not change how the model treats different groups, and it makes fairness harder for others to verify.

## Key idea
Model cards support transparency; keeping training data, limitations and intended use secret mainly costs trust and accountability.
Q000191:
## What an AI governance board does
An AI governance board sets the rules for how a company builds, buys and uses AI: which use cases are allowed, what risk reviews are required, who approves launches and how incidents are handled.
AI risk is not purely technical. One hiring model can raise at the same time:
- **Legal and compliance** questions: anti-discrimination law, the EU AI Act, privacy rules.
- **Security** questions: who can access the model and the training data.
- **Business** questions: is the use case worth it, who owns the outcome.
- **Technical** questions: accuracy, bias testing, monitoring.
## Example
A data science team sees a model with 92% accuracy and wants to ship it. Legal notices the training data includes personal data collected for a different purpose, and the business owner notices it will affect customers in a regulated market. Only a board with all of these views catches every issue before launch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CIO only:** one executive can decide fast but brings a single perspective, so legal, ethical and business risks outside that role's expertise go unnoticed.
- ✗ **B. Data science only:** the team understands models well but is not equipped to judge regulatory exposure, contract terms or business impact, and it would be reviewing its own work.
- ✓ **C. Cross-functional leaders (correct):** legal, compliance, security, business and technical members each see a different class of risk, so decisions are balanced and have owners across the company.
- ✗ **D. External consultants only:** outsiders can advise, but governance needs internal owners who are accountable for decisions and who stay after the engagement ends.

## Key idea
AI governance needs cross-functional membership because AI risks span legal, security, business and technical areas; any single-group board has blind spots.
Q000192:
## Why AI rules differ by jurisdiction
AI regulation is not global. The same system can be lawful in one country and restricted in another.
- **EU AI Act**: classifies AI systems by risk. AI used in employment, such as screening or ranking job applicants, is listed as **high-risk**, which brings obligations such as risk management, data governance, technical documentation, human oversight and logging.
- **United States**: there is no single federal AI law; rules come from existing anti-discrimination law and from state and city laws. For example, New York City requires bias audits and candidate notices for automated employment decision tools.
## What a jurisdiction-specific review does
Before launch, legal and compliance teams map each deployment region to its rules, then list the controls each region needs (documentation, notices, bias audits, human review). The model may stay the same while the surrounding process changes per region.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Documentation on request:** the EU AI Act expects high-risk systems to have technical documentation before they are placed on the market and to keep logs while in use; producing records only after a regulator asks is itself a compliance failure.
- ✗ **B. Vendor terms of service:** the deploying company remains responsible for how it uses the tool in hiring; a vendor's terms cover the vendor's obligations, not the customer's legal duties.
- ✗ **C. Identical configuration everywhere:** one setup with no local review ignores region-specific requirements such as notices, audits or human oversight, so some regions are likely non-compliant.
- ✓ **D. Jurisdiction-specific review (correct):** it identifies the concrete obligations in each region, such as the EU AI Act high-risk requirements for hiring tools, before the tool goes live, which is where compliance risk is actually reduced.

## Key idea
Compliance risk is reduced by reviewing each jurisdiction's rules before deployment, not by relying on vendors, one global setup or documentation after the fact.
Q000193:
## Controlling who can call a model
In Amazon Bedrock, invoking a model is an API call such as `bedrock:InvokeModel` or `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream`. **IAM** policies decide who may make it.
- Attach a policy that allows `bedrock:InvokeModel` only to a data science role or group.
- Scope it to specific models with the model's ARN, for example `arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/<model-id>`.
- Everyone else gets an access denied error.
## Recording who called it
**AWS CloudTrail** records Bedrock API calls, including model invocations: which identity called, which model, when and from where. Event history keeps recent events for 90 days; for long-term audit, a trail delivers the records to an S3 bucket, or a CloudTrail Lake event data store keeps them for querying.
Bedrock also offers **model invocation logging**, which can store the prompt and response content in CloudWatch Logs or S3 when the audit also needs to see what was asked.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Public unauthenticated access:** anyone on the internet could use the model, which is the opposite of restricting access, and calls could not be tied to a person.
- ✗ **B. Disabling logging:** removing logs saves little storage cost and destroys the audit evidence the requirement explicitly asks for.
- ✗ **C. Shared root credentials:** the root user has unrestricted access, and sharing one credential makes it impossible to know which person made a call; AWS best practice is to not use root for daily work at all.
- ✓ **D. IAM plus CloudTrail (correct):** IAM enforces least-privilege access so only the authorized team can invoke the model, and CloudTrail provides the audit trail of every call and the identity that made it.

## Key idea
Governance of model access means authorize with IAM (who may call) and audit with CloudTrail (who did call), per individual identity.
Q000194:
## Risk tiering for AI
Risk tiering sorts AI systems into levels, such as low, medium and high, so the strictest reviews go where failure hurts most. The main question is: **if this system is wrong or unfair, who gets hurt and how badly?**
Factors that raise a system's tier:
- It makes or strongly influences decisions about people: hiring, credit, insurance, healthcare, education.
- Errors affect safety, legal rights or access to essential services.
- Decisions are automated with little human review, or are hard to reverse.
## Example
An internal tool that drafts meeting summaries is low risk: a bad summary is annoying and easy to fix. A model that decides who gets a loan is high risk: a biased result can deny people access to credit. This matches how the EU AI Act assigns its high-risk category by use case, not by technology.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Model newness:** a new model may be less proven, but a new model drafting marketing slogans is still low risk while an old one scoring loan applicants is high risk; the use case matters more.
- ✗ **B. Team size:** the number of developers says nothing about what happens to people when the system fails.
- ✗ **C. Lines of code:** code size measures engineering effort, not impact; a short script can make high-stakes decisions.
- ✓ **D. Potential harm to people (correct):** the impact on rights, safety or access to services is what makes an AI system risky, so it should drive the tier and the amount of oversight.

## Key idea
Tier AI systems by the harm a failure could cause to people, not by technical attributes such as model age, team size or code volume.
Q000195:
## Pillars and lenses
The **AWS Well-Architected Framework** has six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. They apply to any workload.
A **lens** extends the framework for a specific domain. It adds domain-specific questions and best practices that you review alongside the pillars, for example in the AWS Well-Architected Tool. AWS publishes lenses for areas such as serverless, machine learning and generative AI.
## What the Responsible AI Lens adds
The Responsible AI Lens adds guidance for building AI responsibly, grounded in AWS's responsible AI dimensions: fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance and transparency. Its best practices help you, for example, define a system's intended use and risks, evaluate it for bias and keep appropriate human oversight.
- The core pillars still apply: security, reliability and cost remain important.
- The lens layers AI-specific considerations on top instead of replacing anything.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Replaces the security pillar:** lenses never remove a pillar; security still applies to AI workloads, and responsible-AI topics are added alongside it.
- ✗ **B. Cost optimization only:** the lens is about responsible AI dimensions such as fairness and transparency, not spending; cost remains the job of the cost optimization pillar.
- ✓ **C. Adds responsible-AI guidance on top (correct):** like other lenses, it supplements the core pillars with domain-specific best practices rather than replacing or narrowing them.
- ✗ **D. Only outside AWS:** the lens is meant for reviewing AI workloads, including those built on AWS, with the same Well-Architected process.

## Key idea
A Well-Architected lens extends the six pillars for a domain; the Responsible AI Lens adds responsible-AI questions while every pillar still applies.
Q000196:
## Shadow AI and missing governance
**Shadow AI** is AI adopted by teams without central visibility or approval, for example a department signing up for a chatbot service and pasting customer data into it.
An enterprise AI governance program usually includes:
- **Intake**: every new AI use case is registered with its purpose, data and owner.
- **Review and approval**: risk, legal, security and privacy checks scaled to the risk tier.
- **Policies and standards**: approved tools, allowed data classes, required logging.
- **Inventory and monitoring**: a list of all AI systems in use and their status.
## Example
Marketing sends customer emails to one external AI service, while finance uses another that keeps prompts for training. Neither went through review, so data handling differs and nobody has the full picture. That is the situation an audit finds when intake and approval do not exist.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Overinvestment in monitoring:** the problem is the lack of oversight; strong monitoring would have surfaced these deployments earlier.
- ✗ **B. Excessive centralization:** too much central control causes slow approvals, not teams deploying freely with no review; the finding shows the opposite.
- ✗ **C. Governance fine, needs compute:** compute capacity has nothing to do with unreviewed deployments and inconsistent data handling, which are process failures.
- ✓ **D. No enterprise governance with intake and approval (correct):** units deploying tools independently, with inconsistent data handling, is the typical symptom of having no central process to register, review and approve AI use.

## Key idea
Unreviewed AI tools across business units signal missing enterprise governance, fixed by an intake, review and approval process with a central inventory.
Q000197:
## Two ways to organize AI governance
- **Centralized**: one team, often an AI Center of Excellence or governance office, reviews and approves every use case. Standards are applied the same way everywhere, but the team can become a bottleneck as requests grow.
- **Federated**: the enterprise sets guardrails (policies, risk tiers, approved tools, required controls), and business units approve their own use cases within them. Teams move faster, but results depend on how well each unit follows the guardrails.
## Example
With 20 use cases a year, a central team can review each one. With 500, requests queue for months and teams may bypass the process. Many companies end up with a hybrid: high-risk use cases go to the central board, lower-risk ones are approved locally under enterprise standards.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Centralized costs more infrastructure:** governance models are about decision processes, not cloud spend; neither model inherently changes infrastructure fees.
- ✓ **B. Consistency versus speed (correct):** centralized governance gives uniform oversight but can slow innovation, while federated governance is faster but needs strong enterprise guardrails to stay consistent.
- ✗ **C. Federated removes compliance review:** federated governance moves reviews to business units under enterprise rules; compliance obligations remain.
- ✗ **D. No difference:** the two models differ in who decides, how fast decisions happen and how consistent they are.

## Key idea
Centralized governance trades speed for consistency; federated governance trades consistency for speed and relies on strong shared guardrails.
Q000198:
## Continuous compliance evidence on AWS
**AWS Config** records the configuration of AWS resources, keeps a timeline of every change, and evaluates resources against **rules** that express your controls, for example "S3 buckets holding training data must block public access" or "SageMaker notebook instances must not have direct internet access".
- A **conformance pack** bundles a set of rules and remediation actions into one deployable unit, so a whole control set (a standard or your internal controls) can be applied across accounts and Regions with AWS Organizations.
- For every resource and rule, Config records compliant or noncompliant results over time, which gives auditors ongoing evidence instead of point-in-time screenshots.
- Results can be aggregated across accounts and exported or queried for audit reports.
## Where Audit Manager fits
AWS Audit Manager used to be the usual answer for control-mapped audit evidence, but it has been closed to new customers since April 30, 2026; AWS points new users to AWS Config conformance packs, whose rule evaluations were already one of Audit Manager's evidence sources.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Artifact:** it provides AWS's own compliance reports and agreements, such as SOC and ISO reports, which describe AWS's controls, not evidence about the customer's own workloads.
- ✗ **B. AWS Trusted Advisor:** it runs AWS-defined best-practice checks for cost, security and service limits, but you cannot load your internal controls into it, and it does not keep a per-resource compliance timeline.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Inspector:** it scans EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and network exposure; it does not evaluate resources against your own control set or keep compliance history per control.
- ✓ **D. AWS Config (correct):** its rules and conformance packs continuously evaluate the AI workloads' resources against the internal controls, grouped by control set, and it keeps each resource's configuration and compliance history as ongoing evidence.

## Key idea
Customer-side, continuously recorded compliance evidence against your own controls comes from AWS Config and conformance packs; AWS's own compliance reports come from Artifact.
Q000199:
## Proxy variables
Removing a protected attribute, such as gender or ethnicity, from training data is sometimes called "fairness through unawareness". It often does not work, because other features are **correlated** with the removed attribute and let the model infer it anyway. These features are called **proxy variables**.
Common proxies:
- ZIP code or neighborhood, which can correlate with ethnicity.
- Name of school or university attended.
- Gaps in employment history, which can correlate with gender or caregiving.
## How to detect and fix it
Keep the protected attribute aside for **evaluation**, then compare outcomes such as selection rates across groups. Tools like Amazon SageMaker Clarify compute bias metrics before and after training. Fixes include removing or transforming strong proxies, rebalancing data and adding human review.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Proxy variables (correct):** features that correlate with the removed attribute let the model reproduce the same unfair pattern, which explains biased outcomes even when the attribute is absent.
- ✗ **B. Insufficient compute:** too little compute makes training slow or inference fail; it does not make predictions systematically unfavorable to one group.
- ✗ **C. Data drift:** drift means production inputs change over time; the described problem is a consistent group disparity in how the model decides, not a shift after deployment.
- ✗ **D. Software bug:** a bug would not usually target one demographic group consistently; a systematic group disparity is the signature of learned bias.

## Key idea
Dropping a protected attribute does not remove bias when proxy variables remain; measure outcomes by group to detect it.
Q000200:
## Where bias enters the ML lifecycle
Bias can enter at several stages: data collection, labeling, feature choice, training, evaluation and deployment. A frequent starting point is **representation bias**: a group appears in training data far less than in the real population.
## Why under-representation matters
A model learns patterns from examples. If a segment is 3% of the training data but 20% of applicants:
- The model sees few examples of that segment repaying loans, so its estimates for them are less reliable.
- Overall accuracy can still look good, because the metric is dominated by the majority group.
- Errors concentrate on the under-represented segment, for example more wrongful rejections.
## Fixes
Collect more representative data, rebalance or reweight samples, and measure bias before training (for example, class imbalance metrics in Amazon SageMaker Clarify) and again on the trained model.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Monitoring refresh rate:** a slow dashboard can delay noticing a problem, but it cannot change which applicants the model approves.
- ✗ **B. Pricing:** the cost per prediction affects the bill, not the model's decisions.
- ✓ **C. Data collection (correct):** the segment's share of training data (3%) is far below its share of applicants (20%), so the model learned from an unrepresentative sample; that is where the bias started.
- ✗ **D. Endpoint instance type:** instance type changes latency and throughput; the same model gives the same predictions on any instance type.

## Key idea
When a group is far rarer in training data than in reality, bias was introduced at data collection; infrastructure and pricing do not change model decisions.
Q000201:
## IP risk in generative AI outputs
Generative models learn from large datasets that can include copyrighted material. Occasionally an output can closely resemble a specific work, such as a recognizable image or passage. Publishing it could expose the company to infringement claims.
Controls work in layers:
- **Model choice and contracts**: prefer models with clear training-data licensing, and check whether the provider offers **IP indemnity** for outputs under its terms.
- **Output filtering**: screen outputs, for example with similarity checks against known works or filters that block requests for specific artists' styles or brands.
- **Human review**: a person checks content before it is published, especially for external campaigns.
- **Records**: keep prompts and outputs so the company can show how content was created.
## Example
A marketing image is generated, passed through a similarity check, reviewed by the brand team, and only then published.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Smaller, faster model:** size and speed do not decide whether outputs resemble copyrighted works; any model trained on such data can do it.
- ✓ **B. Filtering, licensed or indemnified models and human review (correct):** these directly target the chance that infringing content is produced and published, and shift or reduce the legal exposure if it happens.
- ✗ **C. Fewer API calls:** fewer requests reduce the volume of content but not the chance that a given output infringes; the unchecked outputs remain a risk.
- ✗ **D. Longer outputs:** output length has nothing to do with copyright similarity and can even increase the amount of content to check.

## Key idea
Manage generative AI IP risk with licensed or indemnified models, output filtering and human review before publishing, not by changing model size or usage volume.
Q000202:
## Data drift and model drift
A model learns the patterns in its training data. After deployment the world keeps changing.
- **Data drift**: the distribution of input features changes, for example average transaction amounts rise or new merchant types appear.
- **Concept drift**: the relationship between inputs and the correct answer changes, for example fraudsters adopt new tactics.
- **Model drift** (performance decline) is the result: accuracy drops because the model faces data unlike what it learned from.
## How to detect it
Capture a baseline of feature statistics from training data, then compare production inputs against it on a schedule. Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor does this with data quality monitoring and raises alerts when statistics move beyond thresholds. The usual fix is retraining on recent data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Data drift (correct):** production feature distributions have moved away from the training distribution, which is the textbook cause of the accuracy decline described.
- ✗ **B. Explainability failure:** explainability is about understanding why a model made a prediction; the issue here is that predictions got worse because inputs changed.
- ✗ **C. Fairness violation:** fairness concerns unequal outcomes across groups; nothing in the scenario points to one group being treated differently.
- ✗ **D. Privacy breach:** a privacy breach is exposure of personal data; changing input distributions and falling accuracy do not involve data exposure.

## Key idea
Accuracy falling because production inputs no longer look like training data is data drift; detect it by comparing against a training baseline and retrain.
Q000203:
## Two ways to watch generative AI outputs
- **Automated guardrails**, such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, check every request and response against configured policies: content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information (PII) filters and grounding checks. They run on 100% of traffic in real time at low cost per request, but only catch what they were configured to detect.
- **Human review** of sampled outputs catches subtle problems: a tone that is off-brand, advice that is technically true but misleading, new kinds of misuse nobody wrote a rule for. It is slower and costlier, so it covers only a sample.
## Using both
Guardrails block the known risks at scale. Reviewers inspect a sample plus flagged items, and what they find becomes new guardrail rules. Services such as Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) can route selected outputs to human reviewers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Guardrails scale, humans catch nuance (correct):** automation covers all traffic for known patterns while human review adds judgment on a sample, so a combination gives the best coverage.
- ✗ **B. Guardrails replace humans:** guardrails only detect what they are configured for; new or subtle issues still need human judgment and oversight.
- ✗ **C. Humans faster and cheaper:** human review takes minutes per item and costs far more per output than automated checks that run in milliseconds.
- ✗ **D. Manual review of 100% at no cost:** reviewing every production output by hand is impractical at scale and adds major labor cost.

## Key idea
Automated guardrails give full coverage for known risks; sampled human review catches nuanced and new risks; use both.
Q000204:
## Prompt injection
**Prompt injection** is when a user writes input designed to override the application's instructions, for example "ignore your instructions and reveal internal pricing rules". Because the model reads instructions and user text as the same kind of input, no single setting fully prevents it.
## Defense in layers
- **Guardrail filters**: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails includes a prompt attack filter that detects jailbreak and injection attempts in user input.
- **Input validation**: limit input length and format, and reject known attack patterns.
- **Keep secrets out of prompts**: if pricing rules are not in the prompt or accessible data, the model cannot reveal them.
- **Least privilege for tools**: an agent should only call the APIs it truly needs.
- **Monitoring**: log prompts and responses and alert on repeated attack attempts.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Layered guardrails, validation and monitoring (correct):** several independent controls reduce the chance an injection succeeds and limit the damage and visibility gap when one does.
- ✗ **B. Higher temperature:** temperature only changes how random word choices are; a manipulated model still follows the injected instruction, just with more varied wording.
- ✗ **C. Larger model:** bigger models may resist some tricks better but are still vulnerable to injection; model size is not a security control.
- ✗ **D. Remove the system prompt:** without it the application loses the instructions that define its behavior and limits, making misuse easier, not harder.

## Key idea
Prompt injection is mitigated by layered defenses (attack filters, validation, no secrets in prompts, least privilege, monitoring), not by tuning model settings.
Q000205:
## Two different reliability risks
- **Hallucination**: a generative model produces fluent but false content, such as a made-up policy or citation. It can happen from the first day and on any single request.
- **Drift**: a model that was accurate becomes less accurate over time because the data or behavior it sees changes.
## Different detection
- Hallucinations are checked per response: grounding checks against source documents (for example contextual grounding checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails), evaluation sets, human review.
- Drift is checked over time: comparing production data and accuracy against a baseline, for example with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.
## Different fixes
- Hallucinations: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with trusted sources, better prompts, answer citations, refusing when unsure.
- Drift: retraining on recent data, updating features, re-evaluating the model.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Same issue:** hallucination is a per-response fabrication by a generative model; drift is gradual decline caused by changing data. The causes and signals differ.
- ✓ **B. Different monitoring and mitigations (correct):** because the two risks have different causes and signals, governance needs separate metrics, owners and controls for each.
- ✗ **C. Hallucinations harmless:** fabricated answers can mislead customers, create legal exposure and damage trust; they are a real business risk.
- ✗ **D. No governance value:** lumping them together leads to the wrong controls, such as retraining to fix hallucinations that grounding would solve.

## Key idea
Hallucinations need per-response grounding checks; drift needs trend monitoring and retraining, so track them separately.
Q000206:
## What an AI maturity model is
An AI maturity model describes the typical stages an organization goes through when adopting AI, and what each stage looks like across several dimensions.
Typical stages:
- **Initial / ad hoc**: isolated experiments, no shared standards.
- **Developing / repeatable**: some reusable practices, first production use cases.
- **Defined**: common platform, governance and processes.
- **Managed / optimized**: AI scaled across the business with measured value.
Typical dimensions include strategy, data, technology, people and skills, governance and operations. AWS's Cloud Adoption Framework for AI (CAF-AI) organizes similar capabilities into perspectives.
## How consultants use it
They score the organization on each dimension, place it at a stage, compare with peers, and plan the steps to reach the next stage.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AI maturity model (correct):** it provides the standard stages and dimensions needed to benchmark where the organization is and plan the next steps.
- ✗ **B. Network topology diagram:** it shows how infrastructure components connect; it says nothing about strategy, skills or adoption stage.
- ✗ **C. Single model's confusion matrix:** it measures one classifier's errors, not the organization's overall AI capability.
- ✗ **D. Cloud cost report:** it shows spending, which does not indicate whether AI is governed, adopted or delivering value.

## Key idea
To benchmark organization-wide AI adoption and plan progression, use a maturity model; model metrics and cost reports measure much narrower things.
Q000207:
## Dimensions of AI readiness
An AI readiness assessment usually looks at several dimensions:
- **Strategy and leadership**: clear goals and sponsorship.
- **Data**: quality, access, ownership and governance.
- **Technology**: platforms, tools and infrastructure.
- **Culture and workforce**: skills, trust in AI and willingness to change.
- **Governance and risk**: policies, roles and controls.
## The people side
Even with good tools, adoption fails if employees do not trust AI outputs or fear it will replace them. Signs of a culture and workforce gap: low usage of deployed tools, workarounds, resistance to change.
Typical fixes: communicate how AI supports roles, train staff, involve employees in designing use cases and keep humans in the loop for important decisions.
## Example
Executives approve an AI assistant for store managers, but managers ignore its suggestions because they do not understand how it works.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Data governance:** this covers data quality, ownership and access rules; the finding is about employee attitudes, not data.
- ✗ **B. Financial investment capacity:** nothing suggests a lack of funding; executives are ready to invest, the workforce is not ready to adopt.
- ✗ **C. Technology infrastructure:** the finding does not mention platforms or systems; the barrier is trust and fear among people.
- ✓ **D. Culture and workforce readiness (correct):** distrust of AI recommendations and fear of job loss are people and change-management issues, even when leadership is enthusiastic.

## Key idea
Employee distrust and fear of AI signal a culture and workforce readiness gap, which training and change management address.
Q000208:
## Early versus advanced AI maturity
**Initial / ad hoc stage**:
- Pilots run in isolated teams, often driven by individual enthusiasm.
- No shared platform, standards, governance or way to measure value.
- Successful experiments rarely reach production, and lessons are not shared.
**Managed / optimized stage**:
- AI strategy is tied to business goals.
- Shared platforms, reusable components and standard processes (MLOps, governance, risk review).
- Use cases move from pilot to production in a repeatable way, and value is tracked.
- Often a Center of Excellence or similar function sets standards and spreads skills.
## Example
An ad hoc company has three teams building three separate chatbots with different tools. An optimized company runs one approved platform, with guardrails and templates any team can use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger budgets at ad hoc stage:** budget size does not define maturity, and more mature organizations usually invest more systematically, not less.
- ✗ **B. CoE at ad hoc stage only:** a Center of Excellence is a sign of more mature, coordinated adoption; ad hoc organizations typically lack one.
- ✗ **C. Stronger governance at ad hoc stage:** weak or missing governance is characteristic of the ad hoc stage; governance strengthens as maturity rises.
