- ✓ **D. Managed service or proven marketplace solution (correct):** because invoice extraction is common and not a source of advantage, an existing service delivers results fastest with the least cost and risk.

## Key idea
For commodity AI capabilities, buy or use a managed service; save custom builds for what differentiates you.
Q002172:
## Why ROI needs a baseline
Return on investment compares the situation after a change with the situation before it. If nobody measured "before", any improvement is a guess.
A sound measurement plan for a contact-center assistant defines, before the pilot:
- **KPIs tied to business outcomes**: average handle time, first-contact resolution, after-call work time, customer satisfaction, agent ramp-up time.
- **Baseline values**: the current numbers over a representative period, ideally for the same teams and contact types.
- **Targets and a method**: for example "reduce average handle time from 7.5 to 6.5 minutes in 3 months", with a comparison group of agents who do not yet use the assistant.
## Example
Six months after launch, handle time is 6.8 minutes. Without a baseline, leadership cannot tell whether that is an improvement, seasonal noise or no change at all.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Higher token budget:** spending more on inference raises cost but does nothing to measure value, so ROI still cannot be shown.
- ✗ **B. Larger model:** a bigger model might change answer quality, but without a baseline its impact still cannot be shown.
- ✗ **C. More prompt templates:** more templates may help agents, yet they do not create the before-and-after measurements leadership asked for.
- ✓ **D. Baseline KPIs with agreed targets (correct):** measuring handle time and resolution before the pilot, and agreeing on the target, is what makes it possible to show improvement and calculate ROI later.

## Key idea
No baseline, no proof: capture KPIs and set targets before launch so the value of an AI solution can be demonstrated.
Q002173:
## What "pilot purgatory" is
Many organizations run AI pilots that impress in demos but never reach production. Common causes:
- No agreed definition of success, so a pilot is never clearly "done".
- Each pilot builds its own infrastructure, security review and data pipelines, so scaling means starting over.
- Governance, legal and risk teams are brought in late and block launch.
- Users and processes are not prepared, so there is no owner to run the system.
## How to get out
- **Production exit criteria up front**: target metrics, risk thresholds, cost limits and an operational owner, agreed before the pilot starts.
- **Shared platform**: common, approved services for model access, data, security and monitoring that every pilot builds on.
- **Governance built in**: a repeatable review path for security, privacy and responsible AI.
- **Change management**: training, process redesign and business ownership so the solution is actually adopted.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Exit criteria plus shared platform, governance and change management: clear success criteria make the go/no-go decision possible, and reusable foundations make each move to production repeatable instead of a new project.
- ✗ **B. Start 12 more pilots:** more pilots with the same missing foundations add cost and produce the same outcome.
- ✗ **C. Stop all AI work:** this abandons the value the pilots were meant to create instead of fixing the path to production.
- ✗ **D. Each team chooses its own security review:** inconsistent reviews are one of the blockers; they make approvals slower and unpredictable rather than repeatable.

## Key idea
Pilots reach production when success criteria are set up front and a shared platform and governance path make scaling repeatable.
Q002174:
## Total cost of ownership (TCO) for generative AI
TCO counts every cost over the life of a solution, not just the build.
- **Inference (usage) costs**: most foundation model access is priced per input and output token, or through provisioned throughput purchased in advance. Costs rise with the number of users, conversation length and retrieved context. A pilot with 100 users can look cheap; the same design with 50,000 users costs far more.
- **Data and quality operations**: preparing and maintaining knowledge sources, building evaluation sets, running evaluations when models or prompts change, monitoring quality and cost, and paying people to review flagged answers.
- **Other items**: integration and development, security and compliance work, training and change management.
## Tools
**AWS Pricing Calculator** helps estimate expected usage costs before launch, and **AWS Cost Explorer** tracks actual spend after launch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Inference costs that grow with adoption (correct):** token-based pricing scales with usage, so estimates based on the pilot often miss how fast costs rise as more customers and longer conversations arrive.
- ✓ **B. Data preparation, evaluation, monitoring and human review (correct):** these ongoing operational activities need people and tooling every month and are frequently left out of initial business cases.
- ✗ **C. Office furniture:** general facility costs are not specific to the AI solution and are negligible in its TCO.
- ✗ **D. Price of the AWS console:** there is no charge for using the AWS Management Console; you pay for the services you use.
- ✗ **E. Project manager laptop:** a one-time equipment cost is trivial compared with recurring inference and operational costs.

## Key idea
GenAI TCO is dominated by recurring costs, usage-based inference and ongoing data, evaluation and review work, not one-time items.
Q002175:
## Why loan decisions are high stakes
A decision to deny credit significantly affects a person's life, and lending is regulated in most jurisdictions. Models can reflect bias from historical data, and errors are costly for both applicants and the bank.
## Key responsible AI controls
- **Human in the loop**: a qualified person reviews adverse decisions (denials) before they are final, instead of the model acting alone.
- **Explainability**: the applicant and reviewer get understandable reasons, for example "debt-to-income ratio above threshold". Tools such as SageMaker Clarify can help explain which features influenced a prediction. Many lending regulations require giving applicants the principal reasons for a denial.
- **Contestability**: an appeal process lets applicants correct wrong data or ask for reconsideration.
- **Fairness monitoring**: regular checks of outcomes across groups to detect bias.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Retrain daily:** frequent retraining does not add oversight or explanations and can introduce new errors if data and results are not validated.
- ✗ **B. Fully automate to remove human bias:** removing people does not remove bias, because the model can learn bias from historical data, and it eliminates the oversight needed for high-stakes decisions.
- ✓ **C. Human review, explanations and appeals for adverse decisions (correct):** this keeps accountability with people, gives applicants reasons they can act on, and provides a way to fix errors, which is what responsible AI requires for high-impact decisions.
- ✗ **D. Hide the use of AI:** concealing AI from applicants violates transparency principles and makes explanation and appeal impossible.

## Key idea
High-stakes AI decisions need human oversight, explanations and a way to appeal, not full automation or secrecy.
Q002176:
## Management system standards
A **management system standard** defines how an organization sets policies, assigns roles, assesses risk, runs controls, measures results and continually improves (the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle). An accredited certification body can audit and certify that the system meets the standard.
## Standards compared
- **ISO/IEC 42001** (published 2023) is the first international management system standard for AI. It covers AI policy, roles, AI risk and impact assessment, controls over the AI lifecycle, and continual improvement. Organizations can be certified against it; AWS itself has obtained ISO/IEC 42001 certification covering AI services such as Amazon Bedrock.
- **ISO/IEC 27001** is the information security management system standard; **ISO/IEC 27017** adds guidance on security controls for cloud services.
- **ISO 9001** is a quality management system standard for products and services in general.
- **PCI DSS** is a security standard for handling payment card data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. ISO/IEC 27017:** it provides cloud security control guidance, not an AI governance management system.
- ✓ **B. ISO/IEC 42001 (correct):** it is a certifiable management system standard written specifically for governing AI, covering policies, risk assessment and continual improvement across the organization.
- ✗ **C. ISO 9001 only:** it certifies general quality management and does not address AI-specific risks such as bias, transparency or AI impact assessment.
- ✗ **D. PCI DSS:** it applies to protecting payment card data, not to governing AI.

## Key idea
For certifiable, organization-wide AI governance, use ISO/IEC 42001; the other standards cover security, quality or payment data.
Q002177:
## You cannot govern what you cannot see
Before an organization can apply the right controls, it needs to know which AI systems exist, what they do and how much harm they could cause.
## AI inventory
An AI inventory (or AI register) records each system: owner, purpose, business process, models and vendors used, data sources (including personal data), users affected and deployment status.
## Risk tiering
Each system is then assigned a risk level based on its potential impact:
- **High risk**: affects people's rights, finances, health or employment, for example credit decisions or hiring screens. These get impact assessments, human oversight and closer monitoring.
- **Medium risk**: customer-facing assistants with limited impact.
- **Low risk**: internal productivity tools such as meeting summarization.
Tiering lets governance focus effort where it matters and gives regulators a clear answer to "where do you use high-risk AI?"

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Ban all AI use:** a ban stops the value of dozens of systems and still does not produce the documentation regulators want about existing uses.
- ✓ **B. AI inventory with risk tiering (correct):** it creates the central view that is missing and identifies the high-risk uses regulators are asking about, which is the foundation for all later controls.
- ✗ **C. Hackathon for new use cases:** this adds more AI systems while the organization still cannot see or assess the ones it already has.
- ✗ **D. Single model vendor:** standardizing vendors may simplify procurement, but it does not reveal where AI is used or which uses are high risk.

## Key idea
Start AI governance with an inventory and risk tiering; visibility comes before controls.
Q002178:
## Why chatbots invent policies
A foundation model generates likely-sounding text from patterns in its training data. When asked about a specific retailer's return policy it does not know, it can produce a confident but wrong answer, known as a **hallucination**. In a customer-facing channel, that can create financial, legal and reputational risk.
## Layered mitigation
- **Grounding with RAG**: retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant passages from approved policy documents (for example with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases) and instructs the model to answer only from them.
- **Guardrails**: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can apply contextual grounding checks that flag or block responses not supported by the retrieved source, plus denied topics and content filters.
- **Human escalation**: when the answer is not supported or confidence is low, the bot hands off to a human agent instead of guessing.
## Example
A customer asks about returning opened electronics. The bot retrieves the current policy passage, answers from it, and if no relevant passage exists it says so and transfers the chat.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disclaimer only:** a disclaimer does not stop the bot from inventing policies, and customers may still act on the wrong answers.
- ✓ **B. RAG, grounding guardrails and human escalation (correct):** answers come from approved documents, unsupported answers are caught, and uncertain cases go to people, which reduces both how often invented policies occur and their impact.
- ✗ **C. Bigger model, no human agents:** a larger model can still hallucinate about company-specific policies, and removing humans takes away the safety net.
- ✗ **D. Increase creativity settings:** raising temperature makes outputs more varied and less predictable, which tends to increase invented content.

## Key idea
Reduce hallucination risk in customer-facing bots by grounding answers in approved sources, checking grounding with guardrails and escalating to humans.
Q002179:
## Why adoption stalls
Employees who fear an AI tool will replace them may avoid it, use it minimally or look for its flaws. Adoption is a change-management problem as much as a technology one.
## What works
- **Clear purpose**: explain honestly how the tool is meant to augment roles, which tasks it takes over (for example drafting summaries) and which remain with people.
- **Involvement**: include employees in pilots and design, and act on their feedback, so the tool fits real work and people have ownership.
- **Role-based training**: show each role how to use the assistant for its own tasks.
- **Reskilling paths**: show how roles will evolve and offer learning for new skills.
- **Visible leadership**: leaders use the tool themselves and share results.
The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework treats this under its People perspective: culture, change management and workforce transformation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Transparent communication, involvement and training (correct):** addressing the fear directly, giving employees a voice and building their skills turn resistance into adoption.
- ✗ **B. Mandate usage and track prompts:** forced use plus surveillance increases distrust and may produce superficial compliance rather than real adoption.
- ✗ **C. Delay communication:** silence feeds rumors, so fear grows while the rollout continues.
- ✗ **D. Limit access to senior managers:** excluding the employees whose work the tool supports prevents adoption and reinforces the perception that AI is being done to them.

## Key idea
Raise AI adoption by communicating augmentation clearly, involving employees and investing in training, not by mandates or secrecy.
Q002180:
## Data readiness comes first
AI models learn from, or are grounded in, data. If maintenance records are in different formats at each plant, have gaps and have no clear owner, any model built on them will be unreliable, and nobody can fix the data at the source.
## What a data readiness assessment covers
- **Availability and access**: where the data lives (plant systems, spreadsheets, paper logs) and whether it can be collected centrally.
- **Quality**: completeness, accuracy, consistent units and codes for failure types.
- **Consistency and integration**: a common data model across plants so records can be combined.
- **Ownership and governance**: data owners and stewards who are responsible for quality and access decisions.
- **Volume and history**: enough events, such as past failures, to learn from.
## Example
Plant A logs failures with free-text notes, plant B with coded failure types. Standardizing codes and assigning a data owner per plant is groundwork that must be funded before a predictive maintenance model is feasible.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Outsource with no data access:** a vendor cannot build a useful model without the data, and outsourcing does not resolve internal ownership problems.
- ✓ **B. Assess data readiness and fund the groundwork (correct):** understanding and fixing data quality, formats and ownership is the prerequisite for any reliable AI strategy on this data.
- ✗ **C. Buy the largest model:** model size does not fix inconsistent or missing data; the output will reflect the same data problems.
- ✗ **D. Train on whatever is easiest:** convenient data is likely incomplete and unrepresentative of all plants, which produces a biased and unreliable model.

## Key idea
Before choosing models, assess and fix data readiness; poor data undermines any AI strategy.
Q002181:
## Model lock-in
Foundation models improve quickly and prices change. If an application is tightly coupled to one provider's API, prompt format and features, switching to a better or cheaper model means rewriting code.
## An abstraction layer
- **Multi-model platform**: Amazon Bedrock offers foundation models from Amazon and several other providers through one managed service. Its Converse API provides a consistent request and response format across many of those models.
- **Abstraction in your own code**: applications call an internal interface ("summarize this document") rather than a specific provider SDK, so the model behind it can change through configuration.
- **Evaluation**: a standard evaluation set lets you test a new model against the current one before switching, for example with Bedrock model evaluation.
## Example
A team moves its summarization feature to a newer, cheaper model by changing the model ID in configuration, after comparing quality on its evaluation set, with no change to the application.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Build a foundation model in-house:** pretraining a foundation model costs huge amounts of data, compute and expertise, and you become locked into your own model that must keep pace with the market.
- ✓ **B. Multi-model platform behind an abstraction layer (correct):** the company can adopt new or cheaper models as the market evolves without rebuilding its applications, which is what preserving flexibility means.
- ✗ **C. Multi-year exclusive contract:** an exclusive agreement is the definition of lock-in, the exact risk leadership wants to avoid.
- ✗ **D. Avoid GenAI until the market settles:** waiting avoids lock-in only by giving up the value competitors are already capturing.

## Key idea
Avoid model lock-in by building on a multi-model platform behind an abstraction layer, so switching models is a configuration change.
Q002182:
## Making AI spend attributable
Generative AI costs are usage based and can grow fast. If all calls come from shared accounts with no labels, the bill shows one large number and nobody owns it.
## Mechanisms that work together
- **Cost allocation tags**: key-value labels such as `BusinessUnit=Claims` or `App=SupportBot`, activated in the Billing console so cost reports can be grouped by them.
- **Application inference profiles** in Amazon Bedrock: you create a profile per application or team, tag it, and send that application's model calls through it, so usage and cost can be attributed to that tag.
- **Separate accounts** in AWS Organizations for business units, which also give a natural cost boundary.
- **AWS Budgets**: set a budget per tag or account and alert owners when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold.
- **Showback or chargeback**: report each unit's costs back to it (showback) or bill them internally (chargeback), so teams have an incentive to optimize.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One account with no tags:** consolidating without labels removes the remaining ways to separate spend, making attribution even harder.
- ✓ **B. Tagging, budgets with alerts and showback or chargeback (correct):** tagging makes each unit's spend visible, budgets catch spikes early, and allocating costs back to units creates accountability.
- ✗ **C. Email estimates:** self-reported numbers are unreliable and cannot be reconciled with actual billing data.
- ✗ **D. Cancel all GenAI subscriptions:** this stops spending and the business value along with it, without solving the visibility problem for the future.

## Key idea
Govern AI spend with cost allocation tags (for example on inference profiles), budgets with alerts and showback or chargeback per business unit.
Q002183:
## When everyone has the same model
Foundation models are widely available: any competitor can call the same model through the same services. The model on its own is therefore not a lasting advantage, and prompts or model choices are easy to copy.
## Where durable advantage comes from
- **Proprietary data**: years of your own customer interactions, product data, claims or maintenance history, used to ground (RAG) or customize models so answers reflect knowledge competitors do not have.
- **Domain workflows**: AI embedded deeply into your specific processes and systems, which takes time and know-how to replicate.
- **Customer relationships and distribution**: trust, channels and feedback loops that keep improving the solution with real usage.
## Example
Two banks use the same model. One grounds its assistant in 10 years of its own product documentation and service cases and integrates it with its core systems; the other uses the model with generic prompts. Only the first has something a competitor cannot quickly copy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Publishing internal data publicly:** this gives away the very data that could create an advantage and may breach confidentiality and privacy obligations.
- ✗ **B. Newest model every month:** any competitor can switch to the same new model, so this is easy to copy and adds churn.
- ✓ **C. Proprietary data, workflows and relationships (correct):** these assets are unique to the company and hard to replicate, so AI built on them differentiates even when the underlying model is shared.
- ✗ **D. Same prompts as competitors:** identical prompts on identical models produce similar results, the opposite of differentiation.

## Key idea
With shared foundation models, advantage comes from what others cannot copy: your proprietary data, workflows and customer relationships.
Q002184:
## Why hiring AI is treated as high risk
Automated applicant screening affects access to employment and can reproduce historical bias, for example penalizing career gaps or schools correlated with protected characteristics. Many regulators treat it as high risk:
- The EU AI Act lists AI used for recruitment and candidate selection as a high-risk category with requirements such as risk management, documentation, human oversight and transparency.
- Some local laws, such as New York City's rules on automated employment decision tools, require bias audits and notice to candidates.
Requirements differ by jurisdiction, so a multinational deployment needs a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction review.
## Governance practices
- Classify the system as high risk in the AI inventory.
- Run impact and bias assessments before launch and periodically afterwards.
- Document data, model, intended use and limitations.
- Keep humans responsible for final decisions and inform candidates where required.
- Remember that using a vendor's tool does not transfer the employer's accountability.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Treat as low-risk internal tool:** screening decisions affect candidates' livelihoods and are regulated in many places, so low-risk treatment misses required controls.
- ✗ **B. Use without telling candidates:** many rules require notice or transparency, and secrecy prevents candidates from questioning or correcting decisions.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** High-risk classification with assessments, documentation, oversight and jurisdiction review: this matches how hiring AI is regulated and addresses both fairness and legal compliance across the countries involved.
- ✗ **D. Let the vendor handle compliance:** the vendor can support compliance, but the employer making hiring decisions remains accountable for how the tool is used.

## Key idea
AI used to screen job applicants is high risk: assess bias and impact, document it, keep human oversight and check each jurisdiction's rules.
Q002185:
## The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF)
AWS CAF organizes transformation guidance into six **perspectives**, each representing a group of stakeholders and capabilities:
- **Business**: strategy, business outcomes and portfolio of investments.
- **People**: culture, organizational structure, leadership, workforce skills and change management; it bridges technology and business.
- **Governance**: program management, benefits realization, risk and compliance.
- **Platform**: architecture and engineering of the technical platform, including data and ML platforms.
- **Security**: identity, data protection, threat detection and incident response.
- **Operations**: running and supporting workloads reliably, observability and incident management.
AWS has extended this guidance for AI and generative AI transformation (the CAF for AI), using the same perspectives.
## Example
Building AI literacy programs, defining new roles such as prompt engineers or AI product owners, and managing employee concerns about automation all sit in the People perspective.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Platform perspective:** it addresses the technical architecture and engineering of the platform, not culture or skills programs.
- ✗ **B. Operations perspective:** it focuses on running workloads reliably, monitoring and incident management.
- ✗ **C. Security perspective:** it covers protecting data, identities and workloads, not organizational change.
- ✓ **D. People perspective (correct):** it is the CAF perspective that covers culture, organizational change, leadership and workforce skills.

## Key idea
In AWS CAF, workforce skills, culture and change management belong to the People perspective.
Q002186:
## Activity metrics versus outcome metrics
Executives want to know whether an investment improved the business. Metrics fall into two groups:
- **Activity and technical metrics**: number of prompts, tokens consumed, model size, team size. They show usage or effort, not whether anything got better.
- **Business outcome metrics**: results customers and the company care about.
## Outcome metrics for a customer-service assistant
- **Containment rate**: share of contacts resolved without handing off to a human agent.
- **Customer satisfaction (CSAT)**: whether customers were happy with the answer.
- **Cost per resolved contact**: total support cost divided by contacts resolved, which captures both savings and quality.
Each should be compared with a **baseline** measured before launch. For example, containment rising from 20% to 45% while CSAT stays stable and cost per contact drops from 6 to 4 dollars is a clear value story.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Model parameter count:** a technical property of the model that says nothing about customer outcomes or cost savings.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Containment, CSAT and cost per resolved contact against baseline: these connect the assistant directly to efficiency and customer experience and show the change it caused.
- ✗ **C. Number of engineers:** this measures investment and effort, which is an input, not a result.
- ✗ **D. Prompts and tokens:** usage volume shows the tool is being used and drives cost, but high usage can coexist with poor answers and no savings.

## Key idea
Show AI value with business outcome metrics compared with a baseline, not with activity or technical measures.
Q002187:
## Shared responsibility for a Bedrock application
Amazon Bedrock is fully managed. AWS runs the infrastructure and the model hosting; the customer builds an application on top of it.
**AWS is responsible for** physical data centers, hardware, the hypervisor and host operating systems, the global network, and operating the Bedrock service and model hosting.
**The customer is responsible for**:
- **Access**: IAM policies that control who and what can invoke models, plus authentication in the application.
- **Prompt and context data**: what data is sent to the model, whether it includes personal or confidential data, and encryption choices such as customer managed KMS keys.
- **Guardrails**: configuring Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for denied topics, content filters, sensitive information filters and grounding checks that fit the use case.
- **Output use**: reviewing and deciding how model responses are used, for example human review before sending generated text to customers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. App access, prompt data, guardrails and output use (correct):** these are configuration and data decisions only the customer can make, so they sit on the customer's side of the model.
- ✗ **B. Physical data center security:** securing facilities is always AWS's responsibility.
- ✗ **C. Hypervisor patching:** the virtualization layer is part of the infrastructure AWS operates and patches.
- ✗ **D. Global network backbone:** AWS builds and maintains its global network; customers have no control over it.

## Key idea
On Bedrock, AWS secures the infrastructure; you secure access, the data you send, the guardrails you configure and how you use the outputs.
Q002188:
## Picking a first generative AI use case
A first production use case has two jobs: deliver some real value and teach the organization how to run GenAI safely (data access, evaluation, guardrails, support, cost tracking). The best candidates sit where learning is high and the cost of a mistake is low.
- **Internal users** understand the context and forgive rough edges more than customers do.
- **Human review** means a person checks the output before anyone acts on it, so a wrong answer becomes a correction, not an incident.
- **Low-stakes decisions** such as finding a policy paragraph or summarizing a document do not move money or affect health.
## A concrete example
An employee asks an internal assistant, built on Amazon Bedrock with a knowledge base over HR and IT documents, "How do I request a new laptop?" The assistant answers with a link to the source page, and the employee can verify it. The team learns about retrieval quality, prompt design and usage costs with almost no downside if an answer is wrong.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Internal assistant with human review (correct):** it exercises the full GenAI stack (data, retrieval, evaluation, feedback) while a person stays between the model and any consequence, so errors are cheap and the lessons carry over to later, riskier projects.
- ✗ **B. Autonomous refund agent:** it faces customers and moves money with no human check, so a hallucinated or manipulated decision directly causes financial loss and reputational harm before the team has any operating experience.
- ✗ **C. Automatic pricing for every product:** pricing errors hit revenue and customer trust across the whole catalog at once, and an unchecked model is a poor place to learn how models fail.
- ✗ **D. Final medical diagnoses:** this is a high-stakes, heavily regulated decision where an error can harm patients; AI in this area is normally limited to assisting clinicians, and it is the opposite of a low-risk starting point.

## Key idea
Start with an internal, human-reviewed use case that teaches the organization how GenAI behaves; save autonomous, customer-facing or high-stakes decisions for later.
Q002189:
## Models learn from the examples they have seen
A machine learning model finds patterns in its training data and applies them to new inputs. A demand-forecasting model learns things like seasonality, promotions and trends for each product from past sales.
- When a new input looks like the training data, predictions are usually reasonable.
- When it does not, the model is **extrapolating**: it has to guess with patterns learned from other things, and accuracy drops sharply.
## The "cold start" problem
A product line launched last month has only a few weeks of sales and none of the seasonal history the model relies on. This is often called a cold-start problem, and it appears in forecasting and in recommendations alike.
Common remedies include using data from similar products as a proxy, adding product attributes as features, blending the forecast with expert judgment for new items, and retraining as history builds up.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. No history for the new line (correct):** the model worked as designed, but it had no examples of this product's behavior, so its forecast for it was an extrapolation rather than a learned pattern.
- ✗ **B. Only multi-region products:** forecasting does not require sales in more than one region; single-store or single-region forecasts are common, and region count has nothing to do with the new line's missing history.
- ✗ **C. Larger GPU instance:** compute size changes how fast a model trains or runs, not what it knows; more hardware cannot create sales history that does not exist.
- ✗ **D. Train on fewer years:** cutting history would remove seasonal patterns for existing products and still leave zero examples of the new line, so it would not fix this miss.

## Key idea
A model is only as reliable as the examples behind it; for a brand-new product with no history, weak predictions are expected, not a malfunction.
Q002190:
## Precision and recall in plain terms
When a model flags items (fraud, spam, defects), two questions matter:
- **Recall**: of all the real fraud, how much did the model catch? Model X catches 95% of fraud, so its recall is high.
- **Precision**: of everything the model flagged, how much was really fraud? Model X also flags many legitimate transactions, so its precision is low.
## They trade off against each other
Most models output a score, and a threshold decides what gets flagged. A low threshold catches more fraud (higher recall) but blocks more good customers (lower precision). A high threshold does the reverse.
- Example: out of 1,000 flags, if 900 are legitimate customers, precision is only 10% even if recall is excellent.
The right balance is a business decision. If the board's priority is fewer wrongly blocked cards, precision matters most; if fraud losses were the priority, recall would.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. X favors recall, Y favors precision (correct):** Model X catches more fraud but blocks many good customers, while Model Y's few false alarms mean fewer blocked cards, which matches the board's stated top concern, at the cost of missing more fraud.
- ✗ **B. Terms reversed:** catching more of the actual fraud is recall, not precision, and having fewer false alarms is precision, so this framing swaps the two definitions.
- ✗ **C. Y is overfitting:** overfitting means strong results on training data but weak results on new data; flagging fewer transactions reflects a different threshold or trade-off, not overfitting.
- ✗ **D. Same accuracy, decide on cost:** nothing in the scenario says the accuracies match, and overall accuracy hides the very trade-off the board cares about, since fraud is rare and a model can look accurate while blocking many good customers.

## Key idea
Recall is how much of the real problem you catch; precision is how often a flag is right. Match the metric to the business harm you most want to avoid.
Q002191:
## Training versus inference
An ML model has two main stages:
- **Training** builds the model by learning from data. It is compute-heavy and happens up front or periodically. With a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock, the provider has already done this.
- **Inference** is the trained model answering real requests: every chatbot question, summary or classification is one inference call.
## Why inference drives the monthly bill
Inference cost is paid every time the model is used, so it grows with traffic.
- On Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing, text models are billed per input and output token. More users, longer prompts and longer answers all raise the bill.
- Example: 10,000 conversations a day, each averaging 2,000 tokens, is 20 million tokens a day, and doubling users roughly doubles that.
Options such as provisioned throughput, batch inference, prompt caching or smaller models change the shape of the cost, but it remains an ongoing operating expense.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Model answering real requests (correct):** inference is the production stage where the model serves users, so its cost scales with the number and size of requests and must be budgeted as a recurring expense.
- ✗ **B. Evaluation step:** evaluation measures model quality against test data and runs when models or prompts change; it does not serve live users and is not what "at inference" means.
- ✗ **C. One-time training run:** that describes training, not inference; and even training is rarely a single fixed event, while inference cost continues for as long as people use the chatbot.
- ✗ **D. Data labeling phase:** labeling prepares examples for training before a model is built; it has nothing to do with the model producing answers after launch.

## Key idea
Training builds the model once or periodically; inference runs on every request, so its cost rises with usage.
Q002192:
## Intelligent document processing
Many business processes start with documents: claim forms, invoices, IDs, contracts. Intelligent document processing turns those scans into structured data a system can use.
- **Optical character recognition (OCR)** reads the text in an image or PDF.
- **Structure understanding** goes further: it finds key-value pairs ("Policy number: PN-44821"), tables and form fields.
- Amazon Textract does both, including forms, tables and queries such as "What is the incident date?" that return a specific value.
## How it fits the claims flow
A scanned claim arrives, Textract extracts policy number, incident date and damage amount, low-confidence fields are routed to a person for review (Amazon Augmented AI can help), and the clean values are written into the claims system. Adjusters stop retyping data and spend time on judgment instead.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Document data extraction (correct):** the need is to read existing scanned forms and return specific fields, which is exactly what document extraction services do, turning PDFs into structured data for the claims system.
- ✗ **B. Recommendation system:** recommendations suggest related items, such as similar past claims, but they do not read a scanned form or pull out its policy number and amounts.
- ✗ **C. Image generation:** generating new pictures of damaged vehicles creates content instead of reading the content already in the submitted forms, and would add no data to the claims system.
- ✗ **D. Time-series forecasting:** forecasting predicts future claim volumes from historical counts; it does not look inside individual documents or extract their fields.

## Key idea
When the task is getting fields out of documents you already have, choose document extraction, not a model that generates, recommends or forecasts.
Q002193:
## When not to use machine learning
Machine learning is useful when the right answer depends on patterns too complex to write as rules, such as fraud signals or demand trends. It produces a **probabilistic** estimate that is usually close but not guaranteed.
Some problems are already fully defined by rules:
- A shipping fee from a published rate table (weight band, zone, surcharge) has one correct answer.
- Regulators audit it, so every fee must be reproducible and explainable line by line.
## Why deterministic logic wins here
A rule-based calculation gives the same output for the same input every time and can be traced to the exact table row. An ML model would, at best, approximate the table it was trained on, and any deviation would be a billing error that is hard to explain to an auditor. "Modernizing" would add risk and no business value.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rules learn faster:** rule-based systems do not learn from data at all; they apply fixed logic, so this reverses what each approach does and is not the reason to keep them.
- ✓ **B. Exact, explainable, reproducible (correct):** the fee is defined by published rules that regulators audit, and a deterministic calculation already delivers the precise, traceable answer that an ML model can only approximate.
- ✗ **C. ML always costs more:** running cost depends on the workload and design, and small models can be cheap; the real issue is that a model cannot guarantee exact, auditable fees.
- ✗ **D. ML banned in regulated cloud:** regulated industries do run ML on AWS under appropriate controls; no general rule prohibits it, so this is a false premise.

## Key idea
If the answer is fully defined by rules and must be exact and auditable, keep deterministic logic; use ML where patterns cannot be written down.
Q002194:
## Sentiment analysis
Sentiment analysis is a natural language processing (NLP) task that classifies text by emotional tone, typically positive, negative, neutral or mixed, often with a confidence score.
- Amazon Comprehend offers sentiment detection as a ready-made API, so no model training is needed.
- Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics and Contact Lens in Amazon Connect also report sentiment, but they work from the call audio (or Connect chats) that they process themselves; for text that already exists, a text sentiment API such as Comprehend is the direct fit.
## Applying it to the call center
Because calls are already transcribed, each transcript can be sent for sentiment analysis every night. Calls with a strongly negative score, or a negative trend toward the end of the conversation, go onto a daily follow-up list for supervisors.
- Example: "I've called three times and still nothing is fixed" scores clearly negative and gets flagged.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Object detection on wallboard screenshots:** object detection finds things in images, and a wallboard shows queue statistics, not what individual customers said or how they felt.
- ✓ **B. Sentiment analysis on transcripts (correct):** it reads the text of each call and labels its tone, which directly identifies frustrated customers for supervisor follow-up.
- ✗ **C. Speech synthesis:** converting text back to audio just adds listening time for supervisors and does not identify which calls were frustrated.
- ✗ **D. Machine translation:** translating transcripts changes their language but does not classify emotion, so supervisors still would not know which calls to follow up.

## Key idea
To find emotion in text you already have, use sentiment analysis; other AI capabilities change the format or language but do not detect frustration.
Q002195:
## Hallucination
A foundation model generates text by predicting likely next words. It does not look facts up by default, so it can produce fluent, confident content that is simply false. This is called **hallucination**.
- A made-up "Section 7.4 remote work stipend" is a classic example: plausible wording, no source.
- Risk grows when employees trust the tool and stop checking.
## Grounding with retrieval
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fetches relevant passages from the real handbook for each question and tells the model to answer from them.
- Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can index the handbook from a data source such as Amazon S3, retrieve relevant passages and return citations.
- Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers contextual grounding checks that can block answers not supported by the retrieved text.
- Instructing the model to say "I don't know" when the handbook lacks an answer also helps.
These reduce hallucination; they do not remove it completely, so users should still be able to check sources.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Add Section 7.4 to the handbook:** the handbook is correct and the model made the section up; rewriting policy to match an AI mistake is backwards.
- ✓ **B. Plausible but false content, reduce with grounding (correct):** the model invented a section that sounds real, and grounding answers in retrieved handbook text (with citations) sharply reduces this risk.
- ✗ **C. Larger model eliminates it:** bigger models can hallucinate less often but still hallucinate, so no model size removes invented answers entirely; grounding and verification are the remedy.
- ✗ **D. Model was hacked:** nothing suggests a breach; fabricated content is normal model behavior, and rotating passwords would not stop the model from inventing answers.

## Key idea
Confident but invented answers are hallucinations; ground the model in retrieved source documents rather than expecting size or policy changes to fix it.
Q002196:
## Two ways to give a model your data
- **Fine-tuning** continues training a model on your examples, changing its weights. The knowledge is baked in as of the training date, and updating it means training again.
- **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** leaves the model unchanged. At question time it searches your data (for example a vector index built with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases), puts the relevant passages into the prompt and asks the model to answer from them.
## Why RAG fits fast-changing data
A catalog that changes weekly just needs its index refreshed, often by re-syncing the data source. Answers can reflect the latest data as soon as it is indexed, and can cite the product entry used.
- Weekly fine-tuning costs a training job every week, needs evaluation each time, and still lags behind any change made after the last run.
Fine-tuning is better for teaching style or format, not for keeping facts current.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. RAG reads the current catalog (correct):** retrieval pulls the latest entries at question time without retraining, while weekly fine-tuning adds repeated training cost and still misses changes made between runs.
- ✗ **B. RAG updates weights:** RAG does not modify model weights at all; fine-tuning does, so the description of the two approaches is reversed.
- ✗ **C. Identical cost and freshness:** repeated fine-tuning jobs cost far more than refreshing an index, and a fine-tuned model is only as current as its last training run, so the options differ substantially.
- ✗ **D. Only fine-tuning uses company data:** RAG is one of the most common ways to use company data with a foundation model; it supplies the data in the prompt instead of in the weights.

## Key idea
For facts that change often, retrieve them at question time with RAG; fine-tuning suits stable style or behavior, not a weekly-changing catalog.
Q002197:
## Inference parameters
When a model generates text, it picks each next token from a probability distribution. Inference parameters shape that choice without retraining the model.
- **Temperature** controls randomness. Low values (near 0) make the model choose the most likely words, giving consistent, predictable output. Higher values let less likely words through, giving more varied, creative output.
- **Top P** and **Top K** also limit how many candidate words are considered.
- **Maximum tokens** caps the length of the response.
## One setting, two needs
- Legal drafting wants the same clause wording each time: use a low temperature.
- Ad copy benefits from fresh variations: use a higher temperature.
Both observations are explained by where temperature is set for each team's use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Temperature (correct):** it controls how random the generated output is, so a setting that is too high explains inconsistent legal wording, and raising it is exactly how marketing gets more variety.
- ✗ **B. Maximum tokens for factuality:** maximum tokens only limits how long a response can be; it does not make answers more factual or better sourced, nor does it change wording variety.
- ✗ **C. Embedding size for speed:** embeddings are numeric vectors used for search and similarity; their dimension does not control how varied generated text is or how fast replies arrive.
- ✗ **D. Context window for concurrent users:** the context window is how many tokens the model can consider in one request; concurrency and throughput are governed by service quotas and capacity, not the context window.

## Key idea
Temperature trades consistency for variety: set it low for precise, repeatable text and higher for creative output.
Q002198:
## Chatbots versus agents
A basic chatbot takes a message and returns text. It can explain a refund policy but cannot actually issue a refund.
An **AI agent** adds the ability to act:
- It **plans**: breaks a request ("Where is my order, and can I get a refund?") into steps.
- It **calls tools**: APIs such as `GetOrderStatus`, `IssueRefund` or `SendEmail`, defined with clear inputs.
- It **decides** which step comes next based on results and the conversation.
## Guardrails matter
Because agents change real systems, limits are built into the tools and policies, such as allowing refunds only under $50 and requiring confirmation for anything else. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock Agents are AWS options for building agents that use tools under such controls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Faster model:** a sub-second response improves the experience, but a faster model still only produces text and cannot check orders or issue refunds.
- ✓ **B. Agent that plans and calls tools (correct):** checking status, issuing refunds and sending email require taking actions in business systems and choosing between them, which is what agents with tool access do.
- ✗ **C. Larger context window:** reading longer messages or full order histories helps understanding, but it gives the chatbot no way to act on systems such as refunds or email.
- ✗ **D. Translation layer:** supporting more languages widens reach but adds no ability to plan steps or call APIs on the customer's behalf.

## Key idea
A chatbot talks; an agent plans and uses tools to act, within guardrails, on the user's behalf.
Q002199:
## Overfitting and generalization
The goal of training is a model that **generalizes**: it performs well on new data it has never seen, not just on the examples it learned from.
- **Overfitting**: the model fits the training data too closely, including noise and quirks, so it scores very high on training data but much lower on new data.
- **Underfitting**: the model is too simple to capture the patterns, so it scores poorly on training data and new data alike.
## Reading the numbers
99% on training data and 64% on new customer data is a large gap, the classic overfitting signature. It is like a student who memorized last year's exam answers and fails a new exam.
Typical fixes include evaluating on a held-out test set during development, using more varied training data, simplifying the model and applying regularization or early stopping.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 99% proves correctness:** a high training score says nothing about performance on unseen data; blaming the new data's labels ignores the obvious train-versus-new gap.
- ✓ **B. Overfitting (correct):** the model memorized specifics of its training data instead of learning general patterns, which is exactly why it scores 99% on what it has seen and only 64% on new customers.
- ✗ **C. Underfitting:** an underfit model does poorly even on training data, so a 99% training score rules it out.
- ✗ **D. New data always worse:** new data is not inherently lower quality, and a well-generalized model scores similarly on training and new data; a drop this large points to the model, not to the data.

## Key idea
A big gap between training and new-data performance means overfitting; only results on unseen data show whether a model generalizes.
Q002200:
## Build, wait or use a managed service
A small team with a firm deadline should spend its time on the business problem, not on reinventing algorithms.
- **Amazon Personalize** is a managed service that trains recommendation models on a company's own interaction data (who bought or viewed what), item data and user data. It offers ready-made recipes such as "recommended for you" and "similar items" and serves results through an API.
- The team's work becomes preparing clean data, choosing a use case, integrating the API into the website and measuring results.
## Why it fits this retailer
Clean purchase history is the key input and already exists. Two data scientists can take a managed service live within a quarter, while building from research papers would consume that time on algorithm and infrastructure work. Because the model trains on the retailer's own data, recommendations reflect its customers and catalog.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom algorithm from research papers:** turning papers into a production system is slow and risky for two people and would likely miss the one-quarter goal with no guarantee of better results.
- ✗ **B. Wait for five years of data:** the retailer already has clean purchase history that is enough to start, and waiting years gives up value with no clear benefit.
- ✓ **C. Managed recommendation service on its own data (correct):** proven algorithms, managed infrastructure and the retailer's own purchase history together give relevant recommendations within a quarter for a two-person team.
- ✗ **D. General-purpose chatbot:** a chatbot does not know each visitor's purchase behavior or the live catalog and is not built to rank products for recommendations, so its suggestions would be generic.

## Key idea
With good data, a small team and a short deadline, use a managed service trained on your own data rather than building algorithms from scratch.
Q002201:
## Why long prompts cost more and run slower
Foundation models charge and spend time per token processed. A 300-page manual can be well over 100,000 tokens, so sending it with every question multiplies both cost and latency, even though most of it is irrelevant to any single question.
## Two ways to cut tokens without losing accuracy
- **Retrieval (RAG)**: split the manual into chunks, index them (for example with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases), and send only the few sections relevant to each question. The prompt shrinks from the whole manual to a few pages while answers stay grounded.
- **Prompt caching**: when the same prefix, such as system instructions and fixed reference text, is sent repeatedly, supported models on Amazon Bedrock can cache it. Later requests reuse the cached portion, which lowers the cost of those tokens and reduces latency.
The two combine well: cache the stable instructions and reference text, and retrieve the question-specific sections.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Prompt caching (correct):** repeated instructions and reference text are processed once and reused, so each request pays less for them and responds faster, with the same content still available to the model.
- ✗ **B. Remove the manual:** the model's general knowledge does not contain this company's policies, so answers would lose accuracy and hallucinations would increase.
- ✗ **C. Raise temperature:** temperature changes how varied the output is, not how many tokens are processed, so it does nothing for cost or speed and makes answers less consistent.
- ✗ **D. Larger context window, same full manual:** a bigger window lets the whole manual fit, but every request still processes all of it, so cost and latency stay high or grow.
- ✓ **E. Retrieve relevant sections (correct):** sending only the needed sections cuts tokens per request dramatically while keeping answers grounded in the actual policy manual.

## Key idea
Cost and latency follow tokens: retrieve only what each question needs and cache what repeats, instead of sending everything every time.
Q002202:
## Data quality decides model quality
A model learns whatever its training data teaches, including mistakes and blind spots. Two issues matter most for a triage model:
- **Label consistency**: if one reviewer labels "chest pain after exercise" as urgent and another labels the same message as routine, the model learns conflicting answers and its predictions become unreliable. Clear labeling guidelines and checking agreement between reviewers help.
- **Representativeness**: data drawn almost entirely from one clinic reflects that clinic's patients, language and conditions. The model may perform poorly, or unfairly, for patients elsewhere.
## What does not matter much
Storage location, file format and letter casing are engineering details. They can be changed or normalized in minutes and do not change what the model learns.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stored in Amazon S3:** S3 is a common, secure place for training data; where the data lives does not change its content or quality.
- ✓ **B. One clinic's population (correct):** unrepresentative data means the model may work for that clinic's patients but perform poorly or with bias for other populations it will triage.
- ✗ **C. Lowercase labels:** label casing is cosmetic and can be normalized with a simple transformation; it does not change the meaning the model learns.
- ✗ **D. UTF-8 text instead of scanned PDFs:** plain text is actually easier to use for training than scanned PDFs, which would first need OCR, so this is not a threat.
- ✓ **E. Inconsistent labels (correct):** when reviewers label the same symptoms differently, the model is trained on contradictory targets and cannot learn a reliable triage rule.

## Key idea
Worry about whether labels are consistent and whether data represents the people the model will serve, not about storage or formatting details.
Q002203:
## Style and facts are different problems
- **Style** (tone, structure, word choice) is a stable behavior. Fine-tuning a foundation model on thousands of edited articles teaches it to write in the house style consistently, without long style instructions in every prompt.
- **Facts** change with each new edition. Knowledge baked into a model during fine-tuning is frozen at training time.
## Combining the two
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) searches the current archive at question time and places the latest relevant passages in the prompt. The fine-tuned model then writes the answer in house style using those current facts.
- Example: a reader asks about a tax rule updated last month. Retrieval returns the updated article; the fine-tuned model answers in the publisher's voice with the new figures.
On AWS, both are available through Amazon Bedrock: model customization for fine-tuning and Knowledge Bases for retrieval.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More maximum output tokens:** a longer answer is not a more current one; the limit only controls length, not where facts come from.
- ✓ **B. Retrieval over the current archive (correct):** it supplies the latest editions at question time, so facts stay current without retraining.
- ✗ **C. Prompt instructions alone, no content:** instructions can describe the style but cannot give the model facts it never saw, so answers would miss the latest editions.
- ✗ **D. Retrain from scratch:** training a foundation model from scratch needs vastly more data and compute than 20,000 articles, and its knowledge would still be frozen at training time.
- ✓ **E. Fine-tune on edited articles (correct):** training on 20,000 edited examples teaches the model the house style so it writes consistently.

## Key idea
Fine-tune for how the model writes; retrieve for what it says when facts change.
Q002204:
## A defensible way to prioritize AI projects
Boards accept choices they can trace to clear criteria. A common approach scores every proposal on the same dimensions:
- **Business value**: revenue, cost savings, risk reduction or customer impact, with a measurable target.
- **Feasibility**: is the needed data available and good enough, and does the team have the skills and systems to deliver?
- **Risk**: regulatory, reputational, security and customer-harm exposure, plus how easily mistakes can be caught.
## Example
A fraud-alert triage assistant might score high value, high feasibility (labeled data exists) and moderate risk; a fully automated lending decision might score high value but low feasibility and high risk. Ranking all 14 on a simple scale makes the top three, and the reasons behind them, easy to present.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Most advanced techniques:** technical novelty is not a business outcome and often increases delivery risk; perception of innovation does not justify the budget.
- ✗ **B. Three cheapest projects:** low cost says nothing about whether a project delivers value, so the bank could spend its budget on low-impact work.
- ✓ **C. Value, feasibility and risk scoring (correct):** it compares all projects on transparent business criteria, picks those most likely to deliver measurable results, and gives the board a clear rationale for every choice.
- ✗ **D. Department votes:** votes reflect internal popularity and influence rather than measured value, feasibility or risk, which is hard to defend to a board.

## Key idea
Choose AI projects by scoring value, feasibility and risk on the same scale, not by novelty, cost or popularity.
Q002205:
## Proving value needs a "before"
Value is a change: what got better, and by how much. To measure a change you need the starting point.
- A **baseline** is the level of a metric before the new tool arrives, measured the same way you will measure it afterward.
- For an agent-assist tool, typical metrics are average handling time, first-contact resolution rate, customer satisfaction and after-call work time.
## Example
If average handling time was 9.5 minutes in the quarter before launch and 7.8 minutes 90 days later, leadership can see a measured improvement and convert it into staff time and cost. Without the 9.5-minute baseline, 7.8 minutes means nothing.
Comparing agents who used the assistant with similar agents who did not, over the same period, makes the case even stronger.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Prompts tested during the pilot:** this measures development effort, not the effect of the assistant on support performance.
- ✗ **B. Executive expectations survey:** expected value is an opinion collected before any results exist; it cannot show what actually changed.
- ✓ **C. Pre-launch baseline metrics (correct):** handling time and resolution rate captured before the assistant was introduced are the reference point that turns post-launch numbers into credible, quantified improvement.
- ✗ **D. Evaluated models and benchmarks:** benchmark scores describe how models perform on standard tests, not how this assistant changed the support team's results.

## Key idea
Capture baseline business metrics before launch; without a "before", no "after" can prove value.
Q002206:
## A simple first-year return calculation
Business cases for automation usually compare the value of time saved with the full cost of the tool.
- **Annual savings** = hours saved x loaded hourly cost = 12,000 x $50 = **$600,000**. A loaded cost includes salary, benefits and overhead, which is the standard way to value staff time.
- **Year-one cost** = one-time deployment + first-year running cost = $400,000 + $100,000 = **$500,000**.
- **Year-one net** = $600,000 - $500,000 = **about $100,000**.
## Later years
From year two onward, only the running cost applies: $600,000 - $100,000 = $500,000 net per year, assuming the same savings. One-time costs still count in the year they are paid, even though they do not repeat.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. $120,000 savings:** 12,000 times $50 is $600,000, not $120,000, so the break-even claim rests on a calculation error.
- ✗ **B. Hours cannot be valued:** valuing time saved at a loaded hourly cost is a standard business-case method, and doing so here shows a positive first year.
- ✗ **C. $500,000 net in year one:** a one-time cost is still a cost in the year it is paid; ignoring the $400,000 deployment overstates year one, and $500,000 is the net for later years.
- ✓ **D. $600,000 savings, about $100,000 net in year one (correct):** 12,000 hours at $50 is $600,000, and subtracting both the $400,000 deployment and the $100,000 running cost leaves roughly $100,000.

## Key idea
First-year return counts both one-time and running costs; savings of $600,000 minus $500,000 in costs leaves about $100,000.
Q002207:
## Build, buy, or build on managed services
Sourcing choices sit on a spectrum:
- **Buy a finished product**: fastest, but you are limited to what it does and may not be able to use your own data.
- **Build on managed AI services**: use services such as Amazon Bedrock or Amazon SageMaker AI (and purpose-built services like Amazon Textract or Amazon Comprehend) with your own data. The provider runs the models and infrastructure; your team designs the workflow.
- **Build from scratch**: train your own models or even a foundation model. Maximum control, but it needs large specialist teams, data and budget.
## Matching the insurer's situation
Strong claims data is the insurer's advantage. Two ML engineers and a six-month goal rule out large custom research, and since the insurer does not sell AI products, owning every layer adds no competitive value.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Wait to hire twenty scientists:** delaying for a large research team misses the six-month goal, and custom research is unnecessary when managed services already cover triage needs.
- ✗ **B. Closed product that ignores its data:** avoiding integration throws away the insurer's main advantage, its own claims history, and leaves triage generic.
- ✓ **C. Managed AWS services with its own claims data (correct):** a small team can deliver within six months while still using its differentiating data, balancing speed, cost and fit.
- ✗ **D. Proprietary foundation model from scratch:** building a foundation model needs enormous data, compute and specialist talent, far beyond two engineers and six months, for a company that does not sell AI.

## Key idea
With good data, a small team and a short timeline, build on managed services with your own data rather than buying blind or building from scratch.
Q002208:
## Where competitive advantage comes from
When two companies use the same public foundation model, the model itself is not the differentiator. Anyone can access it. What differs is everything around it:
- **Proprietary data**: order history, product details and past support cases supplied to the model, for example through retrieval.
- **Workflow integration**: the assistant can look up an order, open a ticket or hand off to a human at the right moment.
- **Prompt design and evaluation**: tuned instructions, guardrails and continuous testing against real customer questions.
## Example
Asked "Where is my replacement?", one assistant replies generically. The other retrieves the customer's order, sees the shipment date and answers with a tracking link. Same model, very different satisfaction.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Different AWS Region:** Region choice affects latency, data residency and service availability, but the same model behaves the same way and does not answer better because of the Region.
- ✗ **B. Friendlier brand name:** branding may help adoption, but it does not change the quality or relevance of the answers that drive satisfaction.
- ✗ **C. Higher per-token price:** the same model version produces answers of the same quality regardless of what a customer pays; price differences reflect contracts or throughput options, not smarter answers.
- ✓ **D. Integration with its own data and workflows (correct):** grounding the same model in customer history, product data and support processes produces more relevant, actionable answers, which competitors cannot easily copy.

## Key idea
When everyone can use the same model, differentiation comes from your data, integrations and workflows, not from the model itself.
Q002209:
## Strategy starts with business outcomes
An AI strategy answers "which business results do we need to improve, and where can AI help?", not "which AI tool should we buy?".
- **Identify outcomes**: for a retailer, maybe lower cart abandonment, faster customer service, better inventory accuracy or lower return rates.
- **Find where AI fits**: for each outcome, ask whether AI is a good tool, whether the data exists and what risks apply.
- **Prioritize and pilot**: pick a few use cases with clear value and feasibility, and measure results.
## Why not react to the competitor
A competitor's chatbot may address that competitor's problems. Copying it without knowing whether customer service is the retailer's biggest pain point risks spending money on the wrong thing. Tools and models are chosen after use cases, because the use case determines the requirements.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hire a chief AI officer and wait:** leadership roles can help, but waiting for one person defers the core work of defining outcomes and stalls progress.
- ✗ **B. Launch a chatbot in 30 days:** matching an announcement is reactive; the chatbot may not address the retailer's real priorities and could launch without proper evaluation.
- ✓ **C. Identify target business outcomes first (correct):** starting from the company's most important goals and pain points ensures AI is applied where it creates value, and it frames every later decision about tools and use cases.
- ✗ **D. License the best model first:** choosing a model before defining use cases puts the tool ahead of the problem, and the "most capable" model may be costly or unsuited to the eventual needs.

## Key idea
Begin an AI strategy with the business outcomes you need, then decide where AI fits and which tools to use.
Q002210:
## Activity metrics versus outcome metrics
- **Activity (output) metrics** count what was done: articles generated, prompts written, users logged in. They show the tool is being used.
- **Outcome metrics** measure what changed for the business: qualified leads, conversions, revenue, cost per acquisition. They show whether the use created value.
A CFO cares about outcomes because they connect to money.
## Making the outcome credible
Compare against a baseline, such as leads per month from content before the tool, and attribute results to the AI-assisted content where possible, for example with tracked links or campaign tags.
- Example: "Leads from blog content rose from 300 to 420 per month after we introduced the tool" is a value statement; "we wrote 4,000 articles" is not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Employees who logged in:** logins measure adoption, which is useful for rollout tracking but says nothing about whether the content created value.
- ✗ **B. Prompts written each week:** prompt counts measure effort and usage, not results; more prompts could even mean the tool is harder to use.
- ✗ **C. Average word count versus hand-written articles:** longer articles are not better or more profitable ones; word count says nothing about impact on leads or sales.
- ✓ **D. Change in qualified leads or conversions versus baseline (correct):** it connects the generated content to a business result the CFO can value, and the baseline shows how much actually changed.

## Key idea
Report outcome metrics against a baseline, not activity counts, to show an AI tool's business value.
Q002211:
## Sequencing GenAI initiatives by risk
When two options offer similar value, the difference is risk and what the organization learns.
- **Internal, low-stakes use cases** such as summarizing meeting notes involve staff who can spot mistakes, and an error costs little.
- **Patient-facing content** such as discharge instructions can cause harm if wrong, touches regulated health information and needs strong clinical review, safety testing and governance before launch.
## Building capability first
Starting internally lets the hospital set up the foundations every later project needs: data access controls, evaluation methods, human review workflows, guardrails (such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails), monitoring and an approval process. Once those exist and the team has experience, higher-risk patient-facing projects can move forward more safely.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Meeting summaries first (correct):** with similar value, the lower-risk internal use case lets the organization build skills, governance and trust before exposing patients to AI-generated content.
- ✗ **B. Discharge instructions for fastest return:** patient-facing content carries much higher safety and regulatory risk, and nothing guarantees that such use cases return value faster.
- ✗ **C. Wait for rules in every jurisdiction:** waiting for complete, specific regulation everywhere could take years; organizations can adopt AI responsibly under existing law and internal governance today.
- ✗ **D. Both at once to halve time:** running both pilots does not halve adoption time; it splits a new team's attention and still exposes patients before governance is proven.

## Key idea
When value is similar, start with the lower-risk internal use case to build governance and skills before patient-facing AI.
Q002212:
## Separating the tool's effect from everything else
Win rates can rise for many reasons at once: seasonality, a new product, market conditions, pricing changes. To credit the AI assistant, the evaluation must hold those other factors constant.
- A **control group** is a comparable set of reps who do not use the assistant during the same period.
- Both groups experience the same season, market and products, so the difference between them is attributable to the assistant.
## Making it fair
Assign reps randomly, or match groups on territory, experience and past win rate. Measure the same outcome (win rate) the same way for both groups.
- Example: users win 31% of deals, the control group wins 28% in the same quarter, so about 3 points come from the assistant and the rest of the 9% rise is from other factors.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Count proposals and assume wins:** drafted proposals are activity, and assuming each produced a win is an unsupported assumption that ignores the seasonal upturn entirely.
- ✓ **B. Concurrent comparison group (correct):** reps with and without the assistant over the same period face the same seasonal upturn, so the difference between them isolates the assistant's effect.
- ✗ **C. Ask reps if it helped:** self-reported opinions are subjective and biased, especially from users of a new tool, and do not measure actual win rates.
- ✗ **D. Compare with five years ago:** many things changed in five years (market, products, team, pricing), so the difference cannot be attributed to the assistant.

## Key idea
To prove causation, compare users with a similar non-user group over the same period so shared factors like seasonality cancel out.
Q002213:
## Avoiding lock-in when models change fast
New foundation models appear often, and today's best choice may not be best next year. Flexibility comes from design, not from avoiding models.
- **Common API across models**: Amazon Bedrock provides models from several providers through one set of APIs, such as the `Converse` API. Switching models can be mostly a configuration change instead of a rewrite.
- **Portable prompts**: keep prompts in version control and avoid relying on one model's quirks.
- **Portable evaluations**: keep a test set of real questions with expected answers, and run any candidate model against it. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation can help compare models.
## Example
A team builds a summarizer on one model. When a cheaper, better model is released, it runs the same evaluation set, sees equal quality at lower cost and switches with a configuration change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Multi-model platform plus portable prompts and evaluations (correct):** applications stay decoupled from any single provider, so the company can adopt better models quickly while continuing to deliver now.
- ✗ **B. Five-year exclusive contract:** exclusivity deepens lock-in exactly when models are improving fastest, trading flexibility for a discount.
- ✗ **C. A different provider per application:** scattering workloads adds integration, security and operations overhead and still ties each application to one provider, so it does not make switching easier.
- ✗ **D. Avoid foundation models entirely:** waiting for consolidation gives up value and learning now, and may never end, so it fails the "without slowing delivery" requirement.

## Key idea
Preserve flexibility by building on a common multi-model API with portable prompts and evaluations, not by exclusive deals or waiting.
Q002214:
## From pilot to scale: what the decision needs
A pilot answers "can this work?". A scale decision answers a different question: "is it worth what it will take to run it everywhere?". Executives who disagree usually lack a shared view of both sides of that trade.
A **business case** puts them side by side:
- **Measured value** from the pilot, such as hours saved per shipment, error rate before and after, or on-time delivery change, expressed against a baseline.
- **Cost to scale**: inference and infrastructure spend at full volume, integration work, change management, training and ongoing support.
- **Risks and dependencies**: data quality in other sites, regulatory exposure, staff adoption, vendor lock-in.
- **Resources and timeline**: which teams, how long, and what milestones would trigger a stop.
Example: a pilot saves 12 minutes per route plan in one depot. Multiplied across 40 depots, set against rollout cost and risk, that gives a number executives can argue about instead of opinions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Architecture diagram:** it shows how the pilot was built, which helps engineers plan the rollout, but says nothing about whether the value justifies the investment.
- ✗ **B. Press release draft:** announcing success before the decision adds external pressure and commitments without giving decision-makers any new evidence about costs or risks.
- ✓ **C. Business case from pilot results (correct):** it compares measured, local evidence with the full cost, risk and effort of expansion, which is exactly the trade-off a go or no-go decision has to settle.
- ✗ **D. Prompt and settings list:** tuning history is useful for reproducing the pilot technically, yet it contains no measure of business value or scaling cost.

## Key idea
Scale an AI pilot on a business case that weighs measured pilot results against the full cost and risk of expansion, not on technical artifacts or publicity.
Q002215:
## Efficiency and quality KPIs belong together
A KPI (key performance indicator) is a number that tells you whether an initiative is delivering its intended outcome. For AI tools that speed up knowledge work, KPIs fall into a few families:
- **Efficiency**: time or cost per unit of work, such as minutes per contract reviewed or cost per claim processed.
- **Quality**: how often the output is right, such as the rate of missed clauses, error rate or rework rate.
- **Adoption or volume**: how much the tool is used, such as uploads, active users or pages processed. These show usage, not results.
## Why pairs matter
Measuring only speed invites a hidden failure: reviews get faster because the tool skims, and risky clauses slip through. Pairing a speed measure with a quality measure shows whether the improvement is real.
Example: review time drops from 90 to 40 minutes per contract while the rate of issues later caught by senior lawyers stays at 2%. That is a genuine gain. If the missed-issue rate climbs to 8%, the speed gain is costing the firm.

## Why each option works or fails
