- Cases where the radiologist disagrees with the AI are recorded and used to monitor and improve the model.
Example: the AI marks a small shadow on a chest X-ray that a tired reader might overlook late in a shift. The radiologist looks again, decides it is a real nodule and orders follow-up imaging. The AI improved attention; the expert kept accountability.
This pattern captures the benefits of AI (consistency, speed, a second pair of eyes) while keeping clinical judgment, patient context and legal responsibility with a qualified person.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Show only normal scans:** hiding the scans the AI flags as abnormal removes exactly the cases that need expert review and would delay diagnosis of real problems.
- ✓ **B. Decision support with radiologist sign-off (correct):** the AI flags possible findings to focus expert attention, and the radiologist, who carries clinical and legal responsibility, makes the final diagnosis.
- ✗ **C. Fully automatic diagnosis:** models make errors, can fail on unusual cases or new equipment, and cannot take accountability, so removing human review creates unacceptable patient risk.
- ✗ **D. Avoid AI entirely:** every tool, and every human, makes some mistakes; well-validated assistive AI under expert oversight can improve detection, so a blanket ban gives up real patient benefit.

## Key idea
In high-stakes domains, AI should support expert judgment by flagging findings, not replace the person who is accountable for the decision.
Q002349:
## Few-shot prompting versus training from scratch
Traditional ML classification needs a model trained on many labeled examples, often thousands per category. With only a handful, a model trained from scratch cannot learn reliable patterns.
A **foundation model** has already learned language from huge amounts of text. You can often get it to classify just by describing the task and showing a few examples in the prompt. This is **few-shot prompting**, and it needs no training job at all.
Example prompt for ticket routing:
- `Ticket: "I was charged twice this month." Category: Billing`
- `Ticket: "The app crashes when I upload a file." Category: Technical`
- `Ticket: "How do I add a new user to my account?" Category: Account`
- `Ticket: "(new ticket text)" Category:`
The model completes the pattern with the right category for the new ticket. On AWS, this can be done by calling a model in Amazon Bedrock. As more labeled tickets accumulate, the team can measure accuracy and later consider fine-tuning if needed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Customers classify their own tickets:** customers do not know the internal categories, often choose wrong or generic options and gain extra work, so this shifts effort without delivering reliable automation.
- ✗ **B. Wait for one million labels:** collecting that volume could take years and delays all value, while a foundation model can already perform the task with a few examples.
- ✓ **C. Few-shot prompting a foundation model (correct):** the model already understands language, so a few labeled examples in the prompt are enough to demonstrate the categories and get useful classification immediately.
- ✗ **D. Train from scratch on a handful:** a new deep learning model has no prior knowledge of language, so a few examples lead to severe overfitting and unusable accuracy.

## Key idea
When labeled data is scarce, show a few examples to a pre-trained foundation model instead of training a new model from almost nothing.
Q002350:
## Quality and representativeness beat sheer volume
A model can only be as reliable as the data it learns from. Two properties matter most:
- **Clean data**: errors, duplicates and missing values teach the model wrong patterns. Example: if the same fraudulent transaction appears 50 times through a logging bug, the model overweights that one pattern. Missing income values stored as `0` look like very poor customers rather than unknown ones.
- **Representative data**: training examples should cover the situations the model will actually face. Example: a loan model trained only on customers from one region and one economic period may perform badly in other regions or after conditions change.
Typical practices include profiling the data before training, removing duplicates, deciding how to handle missing values, and checking that important groups, seasons and edge cases appear in the training set.
More data only helps when it is relevant and accurate; adding unrelated or skewed data often makes a model worse, not better.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Many unrelated datasets:** data that does not relate to the prediction task adds noise and spurious correlations, so volume goes up while reliability goes down.
- ✓ **B. Check for errors, duplicates and missing values (correct):** fixing data quality problems before training stops the model from learning false patterns caused by bad records.
- ✗ **C. Only the last week of data:** a single week misses seasonality, rare events and longer-term patterns, so the model sees a narrow and unrepresentative slice of reality.
- ✗ **D. Remove all rare cases:** rare cases such as fraud or unusual failures are often the ones that matter most, and a model that never saw them will handle them badly in production.
- ✓ **E. Match training data to real use (correct):** when training data reflects the conditions and populations seen in production, the model's accuracy in testing carries over to real use.

## Key idea
Reliable models come from clean data that looks like the real world, not from piling on more data or trimming away the hard cases.
Q002351:
## How historical bias becomes model bias
A model trained on past decisions learns to reproduce those decisions, including any unfairness in them. It does not know which patterns were fair and which were not.
Salary history is a well-known example. Past offers may reflect pay gaps by gender, race or age, or differences in how hard people negotiated. If the model learns "people like this were offered less," it will keep suggesting less, now with the apparent authority of an algorithm.
- Removing sensitive fields such as gender is not enough: related features (previous salary, gaps in employment, certain job titles or schools) can act as **proxies**.
- The effect can grow over time, because new offers based on the model become the next training data.
Responsible steps include auditing the historical data for pay gaps, testing suggestions for disparities across groups, basing pay on role and skills bands, keeping a human decision-maker and monitoring outcomes after launch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Preferred font:** page styling is a usability preference that can be changed in minutes and has no effect on whether salary suggestions are fair.
- ✗ **B. Slow suggestions:** generating a salary number from a trained model is fast, and even if it were slow, speed is an operational issue rather than a responsible AI concern.
- ✗ **C. Storage size:** salary records are small structured data such as numbers and job codes, so storage is trivial and unrelated to the ethical risk of the tool.
- ✓ **D. Learning historical pay gaps (correct):** salary suggestions trained on past offers can copy and perpetuate unfair pay differences between groups, which is a fairness and legal risk for the company.

## Key idea
A model trained on past human decisions inherits their biases, so pay tools must be checked for historical inequities before and after launch.
Q002352:
## Every threshold trades one error for another
A moderation model gives each post a score for "likely harmful." The team chooses a **threshold**: posts above it are removed.
- A **low threshold** catches more harmful posts (fewer false negatives) but also removes more legitimate posts (more false positives).
- A **high threshold** leaves more legitimate posts up but lets more harmful content through.
No setting eliminates both kinds of error. Example: at threshold 0.5 the model removes 95% of harassment but also 3% of normal posts; at 0.8 it removes 80% of harassment and 0.5% of normal posts. Which is better depends on the platform: a children's service may accept more false positives; a news discussion forum may worry more about silencing legitimate speech.
Because this is a values and policy decision, leadership should own it, document the reasoning and review it with real data. An **appeal path** lets users contest wrongful removals, which corrects individual mistakes and gives feedback for tuning.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Deliberate balance with appeals (correct):** weighing the real harms of missed harmful posts against wrongful removals for this platform, then providing an appeal process, handles both error types responsibly.
- ✗ **B. Vendor picks the threshold:** the vendor does not know this company's users, legal duties or values, and the company remains accountable for its own moderation policy.
- ✗ **C. Always maximize removal:** wrongful removals silence legitimate users, damage trust and can have legal or commercial consequences, so they are real harms, not free.
- ✗ **D. Always minimize wrongful removals:** letting harmful content through exposes users to harassment and abuse and harms the platform, so ignoring that error type is also irresponsible.

## Key idea
Tuning a classifier always trades false positives against false negatives, so leaders must choose the balance deliberately and give people a way to appeal mistakes.
Q002353:
## Why governance starts with an inventory
An organization cannot oversee AI it does not know about. Teams adopt AI in many ways: models built in-house, AI features inside purchased software, and generative AI tools used by staff. An **AI system inventory** is the central register of all of them.
A typical entry records:
- System name and purpose, for example "resume screening assistant, ranks applicants for recruiter review."
- Business owner and technical owner.
- Data used, including whether it touches personal or sensitive data.
- Vendor or model source, and where it is deployed.
- **Risk level** (for example low, medium or high) and the reviews, tests and controls that level requires.
- Status and next review date.
With this register, the governance team can apply the right oversight to each system, respond quickly when a new regulation or vendor issue appears, and show auditors and regulators what AI is in use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hardware list:** laptops, servers and GPUs are tracked in IT asset management; a hardware list says nothing about what AI systems do, who owns them or what risk they carry.
- ✓ **B. Register of AI systems, owners, purposes and risk (correct):** the inventory gives governance visibility over what AI exists, who is accountable and how risky each system is, so oversight can be proportionate.
- ✗ **C. Office supplies tracker:** purchasing records for supplies are procurement administration and provide no information for overseeing AI systems.
- ✗ **D. Conference attendance catalog:** tracking events employees attended supports training budgets, not oversight of the AI systems the company runs.

## Key idea
An AI inventory records each system's purpose, owner and risk so that governance knows what to oversee; hardware, supplies and training lists do not serve that role.
Q002354:
## Deployer accountability for purchased AI
When a company buys an AI product, the vendor is responsible for how the product is built. The company that deploys it is still responsible for how it is used and what it does to people in its own context.
Hiring is a high-risk use: decisions affect people's livelihoods, and employment discrimination law applies to the employer whether a human or a tool made the decision. A vendor's product may perform well on the vendor's test data but behave differently on this company's applicant pool, job descriptions or local labor market.
Deployer responsibilities typically include:
- Due diligence before purchase: ask for documentation of intended use, testing and known limitations.
- Testing on local data, including checking selection rates across groups.
- Monitoring outcomes after launch and keeping records.
- Keeping humans in the decision and giving candidates a way to raise concerns.
Example: a resume ranking tool rates candidates with career gaps lower, which disproportionately affects caregivers. Only the deploying company, looking at its own outcomes, is positioned to catch this.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only interface training:** fairness depends on how the tool behaves with this company's candidates and how recruiters use it, so it is not purely the vendor's technical concern.
- ✗ **B. Vendor fully responsible:** the deploying company makes the hiring decisions and remains accountable to candidates and regulators, even when the underlying model comes from a vendor.
- ✓ **C. Assess and monitor in own hiring (correct):** the company must check how the product performs and affects candidates in its own process, because accountability for its hiring decisions stays with the employer.
- ✗ **D. Only paying invoices:** paying the vendor is a commercial obligation; it does nothing to ensure the tool is used fairly or legally in the company's hiring.

## Key idea
Buying an AI product moves development work to the vendor, but accountability for its use and impact in your own decisions stays with you.
Q002355:
## Guardrails on both sides of the model
A public chatbot will meet users who try to make it say offensive things, sometimes to screenshot the result and share it with the company's logo attached. The most direct defense is **content filtering** applied at two points:
- **Input filtering**: checks the user's prompt for categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, violence or attempts to bypass instructions, and blocks it before the model responds.
- **Output filtering**: checks the model's reply before it is shown, catching harmful content that slips through even when the prompt looked harmless.
Example: a user writes a disguised request for a joke insulting a religious group. The input filter flags it; if a clever rewording gets past, the output filter still blocks the offensive reply and returns a polite refusal.
On AWS, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable content filters, denied topics and word filters that apply to both prompts and responses. Filters should be tested and monitored, since no filter is perfect.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Input and output content filters (correct):** blocking harmful categories on both prompts and responses prevents offensive content from being generated or displayed under the company's brand.
- ✗ **B. Larger model:** model size does not guarantee safe behavior; larger models can still produce offensive content when prompted, so they still need explicit safety controls.
- ✗ **C. Business hours only:** restricting hours reduces overall usage but a determined user can misuse the chatbot during open hours just as easily.
- ✗ **D. Disclaimer:** a disclaimer does not stop offensive content from being generated or shared, and a screenshot with the brand attached still damages reputation.

## Key idea
Stop harmful content with filters on what goes into and comes out of the model; size, hours and disclaimers do not prevent misuse.
Q002356:
## Vendor concentration and continuity
When a critical customer process depends on one AI vendor, the company inherits that vendor's risks: outages, API changes, model retirement, price increases, policy changes or the vendor leaving the market.
Good business continuity planning treats the AI service like any other critical dependency:
- Identify what happens to customers if the service is down for an hour, a day or a week.
- Define a **fallback**: a manual process with trained staff, a simpler rules-based system, or an alternate model or provider behind the same interface.
- Document the process and the switch-over steps.
- **Test** the fallback periodically, because an untested plan often fails when it is needed.
Example: an insurer uses an AI service to triage claims. If the service is unavailable, claims route to a human queue with a documented checklist, and once a quarter the team runs a drill to confirm the switch works and staff know what to do.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Assume constant availability:** every service, including those of large providers, can have outages or changes, so planning as if they never happen leaves customers exposed.
- ✗ **B. Move everything to the same vendor:** concentrating even more processes on one supplier increases the impact of any vendor problem instead of reducing it.
- ✗ **C. Avoid documentation:** without documentation, the company cannot recover, switch providers or train staff quickly, and hiding the process from competitors does not reduce vendor risk.
- ✓ **D. Tested fallback plan (correct):** a manual process or alternate model, rehearsed periodically, keeps the critical customer process running if the vendor's AI service fails or degrades.

## Key idea
Reduce single-vendor risk with a documented, regularly tested fallback, not by assuming reliability or deepening dependence.
Q002357:
## Safety first for vulnerable users
A mental health app talks with people who may be struggling, and some may be at risk of self-harm. An AI system can misread a message, give an unhelpful reply or miss the seriousness of a situation. The highest-priority safeguard is making sure people in danger reach real help.
A crisis escalation design usually includes:
- **Detection**: recognizing language or patterns that suggest risk, such as mentions of self-harm or hopelessness.
- **Escalation**: immediately showing crisis hotline and emergency service information, and routing to trained human counselors where the service offers them.
- **Conservative defaults**: when unsure, the system escalates rather than continuing an ordinary conversation.
Example: a user writes that they do not see a reason to keep going. Instead of a generic encouraging reply, the app shows emergency contact options and offers a connection to a counselor.
Other responsible practices also apply: minimal data collection, clear disclosure that the user is talking to AI, and clinical input into the design.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Maximum personal data:** collecting more sensitive health data than needed raises privacy and breach risks and does not address the safety of users in crisis.
- ✗ **B. Hide AI generation:** concealing that responses come from AI undermines informed consent and trust, especially in a health setting where users should know who they are talking to.
- ✗ **C. Longest possible responses:** length does not equal care or safety; long replies can overwhelm a distressed person and do nothing to connect them with real help.
- ✓ **D. Crisis detection and human escalation (correct):** recognizing signs of crisis and routing people to human help and emergency resources protects users when the stakes are highest and AI alone is not enough.

## Key idea
When AI serves vulnerable people, the key safeguard is detecting crisis and escalating to human and emergency help.
Q002358:
## What auditors look for
An audit asks a company to prove that its AI systems were built and operated responsibly. Proof means records, not recollection. Two kinds of evidence carry most of the weight:
- **Documentation**: for each system, what it is for, what data it uses and where that data came from, how it was tested (accuracy, fairness, robustness), the risk assessment, approvals and known limitations. Model cards and impact assessments are common formats.
- **Operational logs**: records of how the system actually behaved in production, such as inputs and outputs (with privacy protections), model versions in use, overrides by humans, incidents and which controls such as filters or approval steps were active at the time.
Example: a regulator asks why a customer was denied a loan eight months ago. The company shows the model version in use that day, its test results and fairness review, and the log of that decision including the human reviewer's approval.
Retention periods should follow legal and policy requirements, so records exist for as long as they may be requested.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Employee memories:** recollection is incomplete, fades and leaves when people leave, so it cannot serve as verifiable audit evidence.
- ✗ **B. Marketing materials only:** marketing describes benefits for customers, not data sources, test results or risk assessments, and gives auditors nothing to verify.
- ✓ **C. Documentation of purpose, data, testing and risk (correct):** it shows auditors how each system was designed, evaluated and approved, which is the core evidence of responsible development.
- ✗ **D. Delete versions and logs promptly:** destroying records to limit what auditors can request undermines accountability and may breach record-keeping obligations.
- ✓ **E. Retained behavior and control logs (correct):** they prove how systems actually operated and which safeguards were in place at any given time.

## Key idea
Audit readiness means written documentation of how each AI system was built plus logs showing how it actually ran.
Q002359:
## From answering to acting
A question-answering assistant produces text. If it is wrong, a person reads the answer and can ignore or correct it before anything happens.
An **AI agent** can call tools and APIs: it can issue refunds, update records, send emails, place orders or delete data. That changes the risk profile. A mistake is no longer just a bad sentence; it is a real action with real consequences, sometimes hard to reverse.
Examples of agent-specific failures:
- Misreading a request and refunding the wrong order.
- Following instructions hidden in an email or web page it processes (prompt injection) and deleting a record.
- Repeating an action in a loop, such as sending hundreds of emails.
Controls that address this include least-privilege tool access, limits on action values, human approval for high-impact or irreversible actions, and logging every action so it can be reviewed and undone. On AWS, Amazon Bedrock Agents supports requiring user confirmation before an action runs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Verbose answers:** using more words than needed is a minor quality issue that applies equally to plain assistants and causes no real-world change.
- ✓ **B. Unintended real-world actions (correct):** because agents execute changes in real systems, an error can directly cause financial loss or data loss, which a text-only assistant cannot do on its own.
- ✗ **C. Slower than web search:** latency is a performance trade-off common to many AI systems; it is not a risk created by the ability to take actions.
- ✗ **D. Formal tone:** a mismatched tone is a style preference that prompt instructions can adjust and does not cause harm in external systems.

## Key idea
What sets agents apart is that their errors become actions, so they need tight permissions, approvals and logging.
Q002360:
## From principles to practice
Many companies publish principles such as fairness, transparency, privacy and accountability. On their own, principles are abstract: a team under deadline pressure may agree with them but not know what to actually do.
Principles become practice when they are **operationalized**, meaning built into the steps teams must pass through:
- **Checklists** that translate each principle into concrete questions. Fairness becomes: "Did you test error rates across customer groups and record the results?"
- **Review gates** in the development lifecycle, such as a required responsible AI review before a high-risk model can move to production.
- **Tools and templates**: model card templates, bias testing tools and risk assessment forms that are part of the normal workflow.
- Clear owners and metrics, so leaders can see whether reviews happen.
Example: a project cannot get launch approval until the risk assessment is attached and the fairness test results are signed off by the review board.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Embed principles in checklists, gates and tools (correct):** making the principles part of required development and approval steps turns intent into repeatable behavior that can be checked.
- ✗ **B. Annual signatures only:** signing a document once a year shows awareness but changes nothing about how projects are built, tested or approved.
- ✗ **C. More inspiring wording:** better language may be more memorable, but it still does not tell teams what to do or check whether they did it.
- ✗ **D. Posters:** posters raise awareness, but without process changes nothing requires teams to apply the principles to their actual work.

## Key idea
Principles change behavior only when they are built into the checklists, review gates and tools teams must use.
Q002361:
## What an AI acceptable use policy does
Employees often want to use AI tools but are unsure which ones are allowed and what data they may share. Without guidance, some avoid useful tools while others paste confidential data into unapproved services (so-called **shadow AI**).
An **acceptable use policy (AUP)** for AI is a plain-language document that answers these questions:
- **Approved tools**: which AI services and features employees may use, for example a company-managed assistant.
- **Allowed data**: what information may be entered. Example: public and internal data are fine; customer personal data, source code or financial results are not allowed in external tools.
- **Prohibited uses**: such as making final hiring decisions with AI or generating content that impersonates real people.
- **Responsibilities**: reviewing AI output before use, disclosing AI use where required and reporting problems.
The policy is usually paired with training and with technical controls that enforce it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Benchmark score spreadsheet:** leaderboard scores compare model capability for technical selection but say nothing about which tools are approved or what data employees may enter.
- ✗ **B. Data center architecture document:** network design documentation serves infrastructure engineers and gives no usage rules for employees.
- ✗ **C. Press release:** a press release communicates investments to external audiences such as journalists and investors, not internal rules for safe use.
- ✓ **D. Acceptable use policy (correct):** it directly tells employees which tools are approved, what data they may use and what is prohibited, which is exactly the guidance they need for safe everyday use.

## Key idea
Employees learn which AI tools and data are allowed from an acceptable use policy, not from technical, benchmark or marketing documents.
Q002362:
## Matching launch caution to impact
Not every AI feature needs the same level of testing. The right caution depends on how much a mistake can hurt people. Credit limits are high impact: a wrong decision can block someone's purchases, damage their finances and raise fair lending concerns in regulated markets.
Responsible options for a high-impact feature include:
- **Complete stronger testing first**: accuracy, fairness across groups and behavior on edge cases.
- **Limited, monitored launch**: roll out to a small share of customers, have humans review AI decisions before they take effect, watch outcomes closely and expand only when results are good.
Example: the AI suggests new credit limits for 5% of accounts; a credit analyst approves or changes each suggestion, and the team compares outcomes and complaint rates with the existing process before expanding.
This keeps progress going while making sure the people affected are protected from untested errors.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Launch without safeguards:** relying on customers to call support shifts the cost of errors onto them, and many harmed customers will never notice or complain.
- ✓ **B. Stronger testing or limited monitored launch (correct):** completing the testing first, or launching to a small group with human review and close monitoring, limits harm to customers from a high-impact feature while still moving forward.
- ✗ **C. Cancel permanently:** well-governed AI can be used in credit decisions under appropriate oversight, so a blanket cancellation based on a false claim about all regulators gives up real value.
- ✗ **D. Launch to everyone now:** competitive pressure does not justify exposing every customer to an untested system that affects their credit.

## Key idea
The higher the impact on people, the more testing or staged, human-reviewed rollout a feature needs before full launch.
Q002363:
## What privacy by design means
**Privacy by design** means building data protection into a system from its first design decisions, rather than adding it after launch. For an AI project, typical practices include:
- **Data minimization**: collect and use only the data the use case needs. Example: a churn model may need usage and billing history but not customers' exact home addresses or birth dates.
- **Purpose limitation**: use data only for the purposes it was collected for and people were told about.
- **Access control and encryption**: only the right people and systems can reach personal data.
- **De-identification**: pseudonymize or remove identifiers when the model does not need them.
- **Retention limits**: delete data when it is no longer needed.
- **Privacy impact assessments** early in the project, when design changes are still cheap.
The idea is that privacy is a design requirement, like performance or cost, considered at every stage rather than a legal notice added at the end.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Build data protection in from the start (correct):** privacy by design means including protections such as data minimization, access control and retention limits in the system's design before development and launch.
- ✗ **B. Encrypt source code:** protecting the algorithm from competitors is intellectual property protection; it does nothing to protect the personal data of the people the system processes.
- ✗ **C. Privacy link after launch:** a website notice added after the system is live is the opposite of designing privacy in, and the system's data handling remains unchanged.
- ✗ **D. Keep projects secret:** secrecy about a project's existence does not protect personal data and can even conflict with transparency obligations to the people affected.

## Key idea
Privacy by design builds protections like data minimization into an AI system from day one instead of adding notices or secrecy later.
Q002364:
## When to re-review a deployed AI system
Approval at launch is based on testing at that time. A system can become less safe or less effective later, so governance programs define **review triggers**: events that require a fresh look.
Two of the most important triggers are:
- **Changes in performance**: a drop in accuracy, a rise in complaints or a shift in which errors occur. Example: a fraud model starts flagging many more legitimate transactions from one region.
- **Changes in the data or population served**: new customer segments, a new country, a new product line or a major change in behavior. Example: a model trained on adult customers is now used for a student banking product.
Other common triggers include retraining or swapping the model, new regulations and serious incidents. Monitoring dashboards and alerts help spot these signals early, and a review then checks whether the system still meets its accuracy, fairness and risk requirements.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Dashboard moved to another monitor:** where a dashboard is displayed has no effect on the model's inputs, outputs or behavior.
- ✗ **B. Rescheduled all-hands meeting:** company meeting schedules are unrelated to how the AI system performs or whom it affects.
- ✓ **C. Change in population or data (correct):** when the system serves people or data different from those it was tested on, earlier test results may no longer hold, so a review is needed.
- ✗ **D. New team member:** normal staffing changes do not alter the system's data or behavior, so they are not a signal that it needs re-review.
- ✓ **E. Change in accuracy or error patterns (correct):** shifts in performance are direct evidence that the system's behavior has changed and may be causing harm.

## Key idea
Re-review an AI system when its performance or the data and people it serves change, because launch testing no longer reflects reality.
Q002365:
## Organizational readiness for AI
Readiness assessments often focus on technology: data, infrastructure, tools and skills. These matter, but many AI initiatives fail for another reason: the business never changes how it works to use the AI output.
An AI model produces value only when people act on its predictions. That usually requires:
- **Process change**: new or modified workflows, decision rights and hand-offs.
- **People readiness**: training, time to learn, and incentives that reward using the new approach.
- **Sponsorship and ownership**: a business leader accountable for adoption and results.
Example: a demand forecasting model is 20% more accurate than the old spreadsheet, but planners keep using the spreadsheet because their bonuses depend on avoiding stockouts and nobody changed the planning process. The model is technically successful and delivers no business value.
A thorough assessment therefore asks: which roles and processes must change, are those teams willing and able, and who will lead the change?

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Readiness of processes and people to change (correct):** AI creates value only when workflows and teams adopt its outputs, and this change management side is frequently underestimated compared with technology.
- ✗ **B. Office Wi-Fi for email:** basic network speed for reading update emails is routine IT, not a meaningful factor in whether the organization can adopt AI.
- ✗ **C. Logo on the dashboard:** branding of internal reports is cosmetic and has no effect on the initiative's success.
- ✗ **D. Desks for stand-ups:** seating arrangements are a minor logistics detail that teams resolve easily and are not what limits AI adoption.

## Key idea
The most overlooked part of AI readiness is whether processes and people are ready to change, not the technology itself.
Q002366:
## Closing the gap the assessment found
An AI maturity assessment scores a company on several dimensions, such as strategy, data, skills, deployment practices and governance. The useful output is not the overall score but the specific gaps.
Here, data platforms are strong, but the company has little experience running models in production. That is the domain of **MLOps**: the practices and tooling that take a model from a notebook to a reliable production service, including:
- Automated, repeatable training and deployment pipelines.
- Model versioning and a model registry.
- Monitoring for performance and drift, with alerts.
- Support processes: on-call ownership, incident handling and retraining.
The fastest way to build this capability is a **focused production deployment**: pick one valuable, manageable use case and take it all the way to production with monitoring and support. On AWS, Amazon SageMaker provides services such as Pipelines, Model Registry and Model Monitor for these practices. Lessons learned then become templates for later projects.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More data storage:** the assessment rated data platforms as strong, so extra storage addresses a strength rather than the actual production gap.
- ✗ **B. Ten complex projects at once:** a team without production experience would be overwhelmed and repeat the same mistakes across many projects rather than learning from one.
- ✓ **C. Small production deployment building MLOps (correct):** taking one manageable use case into production with monitoring and support directly builds the deployment experience the assessment found missing.
- ✗ **D. Stop until hiring a large team:** pausing all AI work delays value and learning, and new hires still need the company's own practices and platforms to work within.

## Key idea
Use a maturity assessment to target the specific gap; here, build production MLOps capability through one focused deployment.
Q002367:
## Shared definitions before cross-department AI
AI models and dashboards are only comparable across departments if the underlying terms mean the same thing. Here, "active customer" is defined differently:
- Sales: anyone who bought in the last 12 months.
- Support: anyone with an open account, even if they have not bought in years.
- Marketing: anyone who opened an email in the last 90 days.
A churn model trained on one definition and evaluated against another gives confusing, inconsistent results, and leaders cannot trust company-wide numbers.
The fix is a **data governance** step: business owners agree on standard definitions (and name any necessary variants, such as `active_purchaser` versus `active_account`), and publish them in a **data catalog** so that every team and AI project uses the same meaning. On AWS, the AWS Glue Data Catalog stores technical metadata such as table schemas, and Amazon DataZone adds a business glossary where agreed definitions can be published and shared.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Remove the field:** dropping a central business attribute loses important information and does not resolve the underlying disagreement about how customers are counted.
- ✓ **B. Shared business definitions in a data catalog (correct):** agreeing on what "active customer" means and documenting it gives every department and AI project consistent data, so results can be compared and trusted.
- ✗ **C. Let the AI choose:** choosing a business definition is a policy decision that the business must make; a model has no basis for deciding which department's definition is correct.
- ✗ **D. Separate model per definition:** building parallel models multiplies cost and inconsistency and leaves leaders with conflicting answers instead of one trusted view.

## Key idea
Align and document shared business definitions before scaling AI across departments, so every model uses data that means the same thing.
Q002368:
## Use case first, with targeted data work
Companies facing messy data often debate two extremes: build a complete data platform first, or ignore data quality and start AI projects anyway. Neither usually works well.
- Platform-first programs can take years, cost a lot and often build capabilities no use case ends up needing, while the business sees no results.
- Ignoring data quality produces unreliable models that lose stakeholder trust.
A more effective pattern is to **pair a focused, valuable use case with the data improvements it needs**. The use case defines which data sources, quality fixes and pipelines matter most, and those improvements become reusable foundations for the next use case.
Example: a retailer starts with a demand forecast for one product category. To make it work, the team cleans sales and inventory data for that category and builds a reusable pipeline. The next use case, promotion planning, reuses that pipeline and adds pricing data.
Over time, the data platform grows in the direction real use cases require.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Years of platform work first:** a long platform-first effort delays any business value and risks building capabilities no real use case needs.
- ✗ **B. Many use cases on messy data:** ignoring known data problems produces unreliable models and wastes effort across many projects at once.
- ✗ **C. Tool that needs no data preparation:** no AI tool removes the need for clean, well-understood data; such promises usually lead to poor results and wasted spend.
- ✓ **D. Focused use case with targeted data improvements (correct):** it delivers value sooner and guides platform investment toward the data that actually matters, building foundations step by step.

## Key idea
Let a focused, valuable use case drive incremental data improvements instead of waiting for a perfect platform or ignoring data quality.
Q002369:
## Why middle managers matter in AI adoption
Middle managers translate strategy into daily work. They assign tasks, set priorities and judge performance, so if they resist an AI tool their teams will too, even when executives support it.
Resistance often has understandable causes:
- The tool changes how their teams are measured, and managers fear their numbers will drop during the transition.
- They were not consulted and see workflow problems the designers missed.
- They worry about their own role or authority.
An effective response turns managers into co-owners of the change:
- **Involve them in workflow design**, so the new process fits real work and they understand it.
- **Define success measures** for their teams in the new way of working, so they are not penalized for adopting the tool.
- Give them training and early wins they can share.
Example: in a claims team, managers help decide which claims the AI triages and agree that team targets shift from "claims handled" to "resolution time and accuracy." They then champion the change to their staff.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Wait for voluntary requests:** waiting for every manager to ask for the tool stalls the rollout indefinitely and does nothing to address the reasons for resistance.
- ✗ **B. Bypass managers:** going around managers undermines their authority and usually increases resistance, since they still direct their teams' daily work.
- ✓ **C. Involve managers in design and success measures (correct):** giving managers ownership of the new workflows and clear, fair measures of success addresses their concerns and turns them into advocates for adoption.
- ✗ **D. Replace resisting managers:** replacing people is disruptive and costly, loses experience and signals to others that concerns cannot be raised, making the change harder.

## Key idea
Win over middle managers by involving them in redesigning work and defining how success will be measured, not by bypassing or replacing them.
Q002370:
## What an AI center of excellence does
An AI center of excellence (CoE) is a small, cross-functional group of experts (data science, engineering, security, legal, business) that helps the whole company adopt AI well. It is an **enabler**, not a replacement for the business.
- It sets shared standards: approved models and services, security and responsible AI guidelines, evaluation practices.
- It builds reusable components such as prompt templates, data connectors, evaluation harnesses and reference architectures, so each team does not start from zero.
- It coaches and supports business teams, who stay accountable for their own use cases and results.
## A concrete example
A marketing team wants a content assistant. The CoE provides the approved foundation model access, a guardrail configuration and a review checklist; marketing defines the use case, owns the KPIs and runs the day-to-day process.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Expert support with business ownership (correct):** the CoE brings scarce skills to many teams, while each business team keeps ownership of its use case and outcomes, which keeps adoption close to real business needs.
- ✗ **B. Approving all hiring:** company-wide hiring authority belongs to HR and line managers; a CoE may advise on AI skills, but controlling every hire is far outside its mandate.
- ✗ **C. Replacing finance budgeting immediately:** a CoE does not take over another function's core process, and an abrupt replacement without a pilot or finance ownership would add risk rather than value.
- ✗ **D. Building every AI system centrally:** doing all the work without business teams turns the CoE into a bottleneck and leaves solutions disconnected from the people who use them and own the results.
- ✓ **E. Shared standards and reusable components (correct):** common guardrails, patterns and building blocks raise quality and consistency and cut duplicated effort across projects.

## Key idea
A CoE enables and standardizes (experts, guardrails, reusable assets) while business teams own their use cases; it is not a central team that builds everything itself.
Q002371:
## Why pilot results often do not repeat at scale
A pilot usually runs under favorable conditions: a volunteer team that wants it to succeed, close attention from the project team, and a process chosen because it suits AI. Company-wide rollout removes many of those advantages.
- Other teams may be skeptical or busy, so they use the tool less or work around it.
- Their processes, data and edge cases can differ from the pilot team's.
- Support and training are spread thinner across many more people.
## What this means in practice
If the pilot team cut handling time by 30%, a less engaged team with a different workflow might see 10% or nothing. Plan the rollout with change management, training and per-team measurement against a baseline, and expect to adjust the process for each group.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More users reduce accuracy:** a model's accuracy does not drop simply because more people call it; capacity and latency are scaling concerns, but prediction quality depends on the data and task, not user count.
- ✓ **B. Different engagement and processes (correct):** the pilot's success was partly driven by a motivated team and a well-suited process, so broader teams with other contexts may not reproduce the results without deliberate adoption support.
- ✗ **C. Scaling doubles accuracy:** rolling a model out to more people does not change how accurate it is, so there is no automatic improvement, let alone a doubling.
- ✗ **D. Vendor refuses multi-team use:** enterprise AI products and cloud services are built to serve many teams and users; licensing may change with scale, but a blanket refusal is not the realistic risk.

## Key idea
Pilots succeed partly because of motivated teams and suitable processes; the main scaling risk is that other teams and contexts will not repeat those results without change management.
Q002372:
## Why uncoordinated customization raises cost
When every team configures the same assistant its own way, cost drivers multiply: some pick larger models than needed, some send very long prompts or whole documents on every call, some duplicate their own retrieval indexes and integrations. Spend then grows faster than the value delivered.
## Standardize and measure unit cost
- Offer shared, approved configurations (model tier, prompt templates, retrieval setup) that fit most needs.
- Reuse common components instead of building one per team.
- Track **unit cost**, such as cost per conversation or per completed task, by team using tags or cost allocation, so outliers are visible.
For example, if one team's cost per request is five times higher, the data points to its larger model or longer prompts, which can then be fixed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stop tracking by team:** total spend alone hides which configurations are inefficient; without per-team visibility the cause cannot be found or fixed.
- ✗ **B. Unlimited customization:** free-form configuration is what created the problem; flexibility without guardrails tends to increase, not reduce, total cost.
- ✗ **C. Remove high-cost teams without analysis:** the highest spenders may also get the most value, so cutting them blindly can destroy benefits while leaving the real inefficiency unexplained.
- ✓ **D. Standardize and monitor cost per use (correct):** shared configurations remove wasteful variation, and per-team unit-cost tracking shows exactly where spending grows faster than usage so it can be corrected.

## Key idea
Control AI costs at scale by standardizing configurations and watching unit cost per team, not by ignoring team-level data or cutting usage blindly.
Q002373:
## Two sides of AI readiness
An organization is ready for AI only when both foundations are in place.
- **Technical readiness**: data that is available, accurate and governed; infrastructure and cloud services to build and run models; security, integration and monitoring capabilities.
- **Organizational readiness**: leadership sponsorship, clear ownership, people with the right skills, processes that can absorb AI outputs, and a culture willing to change how work is done.
## Why both matter
A company with a clean data lake and plenty of compute can still fail if no executive sponsors the change and staff do not trust or use the tool. Equally, enthusiastic leaders cannot succeed if the data needed is missing or scattered. Readiness assessments therefore score both dimensions and close gaps in each.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Same concept measured twice:** the two cover different dimensions (systems versus people and processes) and are assessed for readiness, not as a budgeting exercise.
- ✗ **B. Definitions swapped:** leadership support is an organizational factor, and GPUs, storage and networking are technical infrastructure, so this pairing reverses them.
- ✗ **C. Only technical readiness matters:** organizations do not adapt on their own; lack of skills, sponsorship or process change is a common reason technically sound AI projects fail.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Technical is data and infrastructure, organizational is skills, processes and leadership: this correctly places data and platforms on the technical side and people, process and sponsorship on the organizational side.

## Key idea
AI readiness has a technical side (data, infrastructure) and an organizational side (skills, processes, leadership), and both must be ready.
Q002374:
## Sharing data safely for AI
AI projects need data from many teams, but some columns, such as salaries, health details or customer IDs, must stay restricted. The usual pattern is a **central data lake with fine-grained access control**.
- Data is stored once, in shared storage such as Amazon S3, and cataloged centrally.
- Permissions are granted per database, table, column or even row, based on the user's role.
- On AWS, `AWS Lake Formation` can grant column-level and row-level permissions on cataloged tables, so an analyst can query a customer table without seeing sensitive columns.
## Example
Marketing and data science both query the `customers` table. Data science is granted all columns; marketing is granted everything except `date_of_birth` and `national_id`. Everyone works from one governed copy, and access is auditable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Separate laptops:** isolated copies on laptops block sharing, create inconsistent versions and are hard to secure or audit.
- ✓ **B. Centralized fine-grained access control (correct):** one governed data lake lets teams share data while column-level (and row-level) permissions keep sensitive fields visible only to authorized users.
- ✗ **C. Full access for everyone:** unrestricted access exposes sensitive columns to people who should not see them and breaks least-privilege and privacy obligations.
- ✗ **D. Emailing spreadsheet extracts:** ad hoc extracts create uncontrolled copies, go stale quickly and leave no reliable way to limit or audit who sees sensitive data.

## Key idea
Share data through one governed data lake with fine-grained (column and row) permissions instead of copying data or opening it to everyone.
Q002375:
## Communication in an AI transformation
Employees' main questions about AI are personal: *Will my job change? Will I be replaced? Who will help me learn?* Communication that ignores these questions produces rumors and resistance.
Effective change communication for AI:
- Explains **why** the company is adopting AI and what business problem it solves.
- Is honest about **how roles will change**, including tasks that will be automated and new tasks that will appear.
- Describes the **support**: training, time to learn, where to ask questions.
- Is **repeated** through several channels (leaders, managers, town halls, FAQs) and updated as the program evolves, with ways for employees to give feedback.
## Example
A contact center adopting an AI assistant holds monthly sessions, shares early results, and explains that agents will spend less time on after-call notes and more on complex customers, with coaching provided.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Purpose, role changes and support, repeated regularly (correct):** this addresses employees' real concerns, builds trust and keeps people informed as the transformation unfolds.
- ✗ **B. One email, then silence:** a single announcement cannot answer ongoing questions, and avoiding discussion feeds uncertainty and resistance.
- ✗ **C. Only technical model details:** most employees need to know how their work changes and how they will be supported, not how the algorithms work internally.
- ✗ **D. Executives only:** leaving employees uninformed until the end means they cannot prepare, and lack of information usually increases fear and rumors.

## Key idea
Communicate purpose, role impact and support repeatedly to everyone, rather than a one-off announcement or technical details only.
Q002376:
## Deciding when a pilot should scale
A pilot exists to prove two things: that the solution creates measurable value, and that the organization can run it sustainably at larger scale.
- **Proven value**: before the pilot, the team agrees on success metrics and measures a baseline (for example, average handling time of 8 minutes). The pilot must beat that baseline by the agreed amount.
- **Operational readiness**: the team knows who will support the system, how it fits into processes, how it will be monitored, and what it will cost when usage grows tenfold.
## What does not count
External pressure (a competitor's announcement), commercial incentives (a vendor discount) and enthusiasm alone are not evidence. They can influence timing, but they do not show the solution works or can be sustained.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Competitor announcement:** another company's initiative says nothing about whether this pilot delivers value or can be run at scale.
- ✗ **B. Vendor discount:** a price incentive can change costs but does not prove the solution works; scaling for a discount risks paying for something that does not deliver.
- ✓ **C. Operating model, support and costs understood (correct):** scaling needs a clear owner, support process and realistic cost at volume, otherwise a successful pilot can fail or overspend in production.
- ✗ **D. Team enthusiasm:** a motivated pilot team is welcome, but enjoyment is not a measure of business results or operational readiness.
- ✓ **E. Met success metrics against a baseline (correct):** agreed metrics compared with a pre-pilot baseline are the evidence that the solution actually delivers value.

## Key idea
Scale a pilot when it has met agreed metrics against a baseline and its operating model and costs at scale are understood, not because of competitors, discounts or enthusiasm.
Q002377:
## Context windows and long documents
A foundation model can only read a limited amount of text per request, called its **context window**, measured in tokens (as a rough approximation, one token is about three quarters of an English word; the exact ratio varies by model and tokenizer). A 400-page case file can exceed that limit.
## Hierarchical (map-reduce) summarization
A common approach is to split and combine:
- Split the document into sections or chunks that each fit in the window, such as chapters or 20-page parts.
- Summarize each section separately (the "map" step).
- Combine the section summaries and ask the model for a final summary of those (the "reduce" step), repeating if the combined summaries are still too long.
Every part of the file shapes the final result, because each section contributed its own summary. Including section references in each partial summary helps lawyers trace points back to the source.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Guess from the title:** the model would invent content it has never seen, producing hallucinated and legally unreliable summaries.
- ✗ **B. Send only the first pages:** everything after the cut-off is ignored, so key facts later in the file cannot influence the summary.
- ✗ **C. Raise the temperature:** temperature controls randomness in word choice; it has no effect on how many tokens fit in the context window.
- ✓ **D. Summarize sections, then combine (correct):** chunking lets the whole file be processed within the context limit, and the final summary is built from summaries of every section.

## Key idea
When input exceeds the context window, chunk and summarize hierarchically; temperature does not change capacity and truncation loses content.
Q002378:
## Training in plain business terms
Training is how a machine learning model learns from data rather than from hand-written rules.
- The model is shown many examples, such as past loan applications with their outcomes, or emails labeled "spam" or "not spam".
- It makes predictions, compares them with the known answers, and adjusts its internal parameters to reduce the errors.
- After many rounds, it has captured patterns it can apply to new cases it has not seen.
## A business analogy
It is similar to how a new employee becomes skilled by reviewing many past cases and getting feedback, except the model does this automatically and at large scale. The quality of the examples matters: biased or unrepresentative data teaches the wrong patterns.
Training is different from **inference**, which is using the trained model to make predictions, and from deployment, which is making it available in production.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Writing marketing messages:** promoting a model's benefits is communication work and does not change what the model has learned.
- ✓ **B. Learning from many examples (correct):** training means exposing the model to data so it adjusts itself to capture the patterns that make it useful for the task.
- ✗ **C. Teaching employees the interface:** this is user training, which prepares people to use the tool, not model training.
- ✗ **D. Installing and securing the model:** this describes deployment and infrastructure setup, which happens after the model has been trained.

## Key idea
Training means the model learns patterns from many examples; it is not user onboarding, marketing or deployment.
Q002379:
## Predictive AI versus generative AI
Many business problems combine two kinds of AI.
- **Predictive (traditional) machine learning** learns from historical, often numeric data to predict an outcome, such as whether a device will fail within 7 days based on temperature, vibration and error counts.
- **Generative AI** creates new content, such as text, from instructions and context. A foundation model can turn a failure prediction plus sensor details into a readable note like "Replace cooling fan on rack 4; temperature has risen 12% over 3 days".
## Why combine them
Each does what it is good at: the predictive model gives a reliable, measurable failure probability from structured sensor data, and the generative model turns that result into clear instructions for technicians. Human review of the notes is still wise for safety-critical repairs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Translation and speech models:** sensor readings are not a language to translate, and a speech model converts audio to or from text rather than predicting failures or drafting notes.
- ✗ **B. One image classification model:** sensor readings are time-series numbers, not images, and a classifier assigns labels; it does not write free-text repair notes.
- ✓ **C. Predictive model plus generative model (correct):** a model trained on sensor readings forecasts failures, and a generative model drafts plain-language repair notes from that output.
- ✗ **D. Recommendation and sentiment models:** recommenders rank items for users and sentiment models score the tone of existing text; neither predicts equipment failure or generates notes.

## Key idea
Use predictive ML for forecasting from structured sensor data and generative AI for writing text; pick each model type for the task it is built for.
Q002380:
## What an AI agent needs
An AI agent uses a foundation model to plan steps and take actions toward a goal. To act on real business data, it needs:
- **Tools**: defined functions or APIs it can call, each with a clear description and input schema, such as `getInventory(sku)` or `getShippingRules(region)`. The model decides which tool to call; the application runs it and returns the result.
- **Guardrails and oversight**: clear instructions, limits on which actions it may take alone (for example, it can quote a date but not change an order), and logging of every step so its decisions can be audited and debugged.
## Example flow
Customer asks for a delivery date, the agent calls the inventory API (item in stock in Dallas), calls the shipping-rules API (2-day ground), then quotes a date. On AWS, Amazon Bedrock Agents supports this pattern with action groups that map to APIs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Defined tools or APIs (correct):** the agent cannot know live inventory or shipping rules on its own; it must call systems of record to get accurate data.
- ✗ **B. Removing all instructions:** without instructions the agent has no defined task, scope or policy, which makes its behavior unpredictable and unsafe.
- ✗ **C. Larger image model:** rendering product photos does not help look up inventory, check shipping rules or calculate a delivery date.
- ✗ **D. Higher temperature:** more randomness makes outputs less consistent; delivery dates should be derived from data, not chosen creatively.
- ✓ **E. Clear limits and logging (correct):** bounded permissions prevent unsafe autonomous actions, and logs provide traceability for audits and troubleshooting.

## Key idea
Agents need defined tools to reach real data plus limits and logging to act safely; more randomness or fewer instructions only makes them less reliable.
Q002381:
## What makes an AI business case credible
Boards know that AI benefits are uncertain. They trust a business case that shows its reasoning more than one that shows the biggest number.
- **Explicit assumptions**: for example, "the assistant handles 30% of tier-1 tickets, saving 6 minutes each at a loaded cost of $40 per hour".
- **Ranges and scenarios**: a low, expected and high case for both benefits and costs, such as annual savings of $0.8M to $2.1M.
- **Risks and mitigations**: data quality, adoption, regulatory issues, and how each will be handled.
- **Milestones**: checkpoints where results are measured and further investment is decided.
Stated assumptions let the board challenge the logic, and ranges show the team understands uncertainty.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. List of buzzwords:** jargon without numbers or evidence weakens credibility and says nothing about value or cost.
- ✓ **B. Explicit assumptions with ranges (correct):** transparent assumptions and low-to-high estimates let the board test the reasoning and show realistic awareness of uncertainty.
- ✗ **C. Highest possible benefit:** a single optimistic figure invites skepticism and sets expectations the project is unlikely to meet.
- ✗ **D. Promise of no risks:** every project has risks; claiming none signals that they have not been analyzed, which reduces trust.

## Key idea
Credible business cases state assumptions and give ranges with risks, rather than inflated single numbers or claims of zero risk.
Q002382:
## AI that serves sustainability goals
Sustainability goals are usually measured in outcomes such as lower emissions, less energy use and less waste. AI supports them most directly when it **optimizes operations** that drive those numbers.
- Route optimization finds shorter or less congested delivery routes and better vehicle loading, which lowers fuel burned and CO2 per shipment.
- Similar examples include forecasting demand to reduce spoiled inventory, or tuning building HVAC to cut energy use.
## Direct versus indirect impact
Content about sustainability, such as posts, artwork or translations, may help communication, but it does not reduce the company's environmental footprint. When prioritizing AI use cases for a sustainability goal, look for measurable effects on the goal's own metrics, such as fuel, energy or emissions per unit.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More social media posts:** this increases communication volume but does not reduce emissions, energy or waste.
- ✗ **B. AI artwork for the report cover:** a cover design is cosmetic and has no measurable effect on environmental impact.
- ✗ **C. Translating the report:** wider language access helps investors read the report but does not change the underlying sustainability performance.
- ✓ **D. Optimizing delivery routes (correct):** fewer miles and better routing directly reduce fuel consumption and emissions, which are the metrics sustainability goals track.

## Key idea
Pick AI use cases that change the operational metrics behind a goal, such as fuel and emissions, rather than content about the goal.
Q002383:
## Risks of building on a partner's platform
Building an AI feature on another company's platform, such as a model provider or SaaS tool, speeds delivery but creates **dependency**.
- **Roadmap risk**: the partner may change or retire features or models your product relies on.
- **Pricing risk**: price changes affect your margins.
- **Availability risk**: their outages become your outages.
- **Portability (lock-in) risk**: if the partnership ends, can you export your data, prompts, fine-tuning data and configurations and move to another provider?
## How strategies address this
Contracts with service levels and notice periods, abstraction layers so models can be swapped, keeping copies of your data and prompt libraries, and a documented exit plan. For example, routing calls through a service that offers several models makes switching models easier.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Dependence on roadmap, pricing and availability (correct):** changes or outages on the partner's side directly affect the company's feature, cost and reliability.
- ✗ **B. Executives attending the conference:** event attendance has no effect on the technical or commercial risk of the dependency.
- ✗ **C. Brand colors matching:** visual branding is cosmetic and unrelated to strategic platform risk.
- ✗ **D. Same time zone:** time zones rarely matter for platform services, which are consumed through APIs and support agreements; this is not a strategic risk.
- ✓ **E. Portability of data and prompts (correct):** the ability to move data, prompts and configurations limits lock-in and protects the company if the partnership ends.

## Key idea
When building on a partner, manage dependency (roadmap, pricing, availability) and portability (data and prompts), not cosmetic or social factors.
Q002384:
## Expressing the value of AI
Time saved is only an intermediate metric. Business leaders care about what that time enables.
- **Value of speed**: a report ready 7 days earlier means decisions, such as adjusting inventory or pricing, happen a week sooner, which can reduce losses or capture revenue.
- **Capacity freed**: if 4 analysts each save 7 days per quarter, that is about 28 analyst-days that can go to higher-value analysis. It becomes a real benefit only if the time is redeployed.
## Output metrics versus outcome metrics
Counts of pages, models or installation hours describe the tool or its output, not the benefit to the business. A strong value statement connects the improvement (10 days to 3) to outcomes (earlier decisions, redeployed staff time, lower cost) that leadership can compare with the tool's cost.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Number of pages:** report length is not a measure of value, and shorter is not always better; the benefit comes from timing and effort saved.
- ✗ **B. Number of internal models:** how many models the tool uses is an implementation detail with no direct link to business results.
- ✓ **C. Faster insights plus freed staff time (correct):** this translates the speed-up into business outcomes, earlier decisions and redeployable capacity, which leaders can weigh against cost.
- ✗ **D. IT installation time:** implementation effort is a cost, not a benefit, and says nothing about the value the tool produces.

## Key idea
Express AI value as business outcomes, such as faster decisions and freed capacity, rather than technical or output counts.
Q002385:
## Fairness in AI-driven pricing
Dynamic pricing tools adjust prices using signals like demand, competition and location. Location can act as a **proxy** for protected characteristics: if neighborhoods differ in income or demographics, location-based prices can end up charging certain communities more.
## Questions leaders should ask
- Do price differences systematically disadvantage particular communities, such as lower-income areas or areas with fewer alternatives?
- Could the outcome violate consumer protection, anti-discrimination or pricing laws in the markets where the company operates?
- Which input features drive the differences, and can the company explain and justify them?
- Is there monitoring and human review of pricing outcomes by area?
Regular fairness analysis of outcomes, not just inputs, is part of responsible AI governance.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Vendor awards:** industry awards do not show whether this tool's pricing is fair or lawful for the company's customers.
- ✗ **B. Dashboard load speed:** tablet performance is a usability issue, not a responsible AI concern about the tool's outcomes.
- ✓ **C. Unfair or unlawful disadvantage to communities (correct):** this is the core responsible AI question, because location-based pricing can create biased outcomes and legal exposure even if protected attributes are not used directly.
- ✗ **D. Hourly price updates:** speed of matching competitors is a business performance question and does not address fairness or legality.

## Key idea
For AI decisions that vary by location or group, responsible AI asks whether outcomes unfairly or unlawfully disadvantage people, not about speed or reputation.
Q002386:
## Two EU regimes to check before launch
- **EU AI Act**: classifies AI systems by risk. Some practices are prohibited, high-risk uses (for example, in hiring, credit scoring or access to essential services) carry strict obligations such as risk management, documentation and human oversight, and some systems, such as chatbots, have transparency duties like telling people they are interacting with AI.
- **GDPR**: any processing of EU residents' personal data needs a lawful basis (such as consent, contract or legitimate interest), plus protections like data minimization, security, rights handling and rules for transfers outside the EU. A data protection impact assessment may be required for higher-risk processing.
## Why before launch
Both regimes expect obligations to be met by design. Discovering after launch that a use case is high-risk or lacks a lawful basis can force a shutdown, rework or penalties.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Assess the EU AI Act risk category (correct):** the category determines which obligations apply, so it must be established before the system goes live.
- ✗ **B. Hiding AI involvement:** many AI systems that interact with people have transparency obligations, and concealment undermines trust and can breach them.
- ✗ **C. Documenting after launch:** required documentation and assessments are meant to guide design and must be available when the system is in use.
- ✗ **D. Storing data in many countries:** transfers of personal data outside the EU are regulated, so spreading data widely without regard to transfer rules creates compliance risk.
- ✓ **E. Confirm lawful basis and data protection (correct):** processing EU residents' personal data requires a valid legal basis and safeguards under GDPR.

## Key idea
Before launching AI for EU residents, classify the use case under the EU AI Act and secure a lawful basis and protections under GDPR.
Q002387:
## Permission-aware retrieval
Enterprise AI assistants usually use **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**: they search internal documents and place the relevant passages into the model's prompt. If the search ignores who is asking, the assistant can quote a document the user was never allowed to open.
## The control
The assistant should retrieve only content the current user is already authorized to see, based on existing access control lists (ACLs) from sources like SharePoint or file shares.
- Each indexed document keeps its permission metadata.
- At query time, results are filtered by the user's identity and group membership before anything reaches the model.
For example, Amazon Q Business can honor document-level permissions from supported data sources, so an HR policy draft limited to HR staff will not appear in an engineer's answer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Remove all internal documents:** this prevents leakage but destroys most of the assistant's value; the goal is controlled access, not no access.
- ✓ **B. Enforce existing document permissions at retrieval (correct):** filtering results by the user's identity ensures the assistant only uses content that user could already access.
- ✗ **C. Ask employees not to query:** a policy request is not a technical control, and users can see restricted content accidentally with harmless questions.
- ✗ **D. Let the assistant judge trust:** a model guessing who seems trustworthy is unreliable and unauditable; access must follow defined permissions.

## Key idea
Prevent AI data leakage by enforcing the user's existing permissions during retrieval, not by relying on user behavior or model judgment.
Q002388:
## Two related responsible AI principles
- **Explainability** is about individual outputs: *why did the model produce this result?* For a declined loan, an explanation might show the top factors, such as high debt-to-income ratio and short credit history. Tools like feature-importance methods (for example, SHAP values in Amazon SageMaker Clarify) support this.
- **Transparency** is about openness regarding AI use overall: telling people when they are interacting with AI, where AI is used in decisions, what data it relies on, and its known limitations. Documents like model cards and AI service cards support transparency.
## How they fit together
A bank is transparent when it discloses that credit decisions are AI-assisted and describes the model's purpose and limits; it is explainable when it can tell a specific applicant the main reasons for their result.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Definitions reversed:** where AI is used is transparency, and the reasons behind an individual prediction are explainability, so this pairing swaps them.
- ✗ **B. Both mean encryption:** encryption protects data and models from unauthorized access; it is a security control, not a way to explain or disclose AI use.
- ✗ **C. Both mean publishing source code:** open-sourcing is neither required nor sufficient; a published algorithm does not explain an individual decision, and transparency can be achieved without releasing code.
- ✓ **D. Why an output versus openness about AI use (correct):** explainability addresses the reasons behind a specific prediction, and transparency addresses disclosure of how and where AI is used.

## Key idea
Explainability answers why a specific output happened; transparency is openness about how and where AI is used.
Q002389:
## Measuring an upskilling program
Training programs are often reported with **activity metrics** (logins, hours of content, certificates issued). These are easy to count but show only that training exists or was touched, not that it changed how people work.
## Outcome-based indicators
A meaningful measure looks at behavior and results:
- Are employees using AI tools in their real tasks, and how often?
- Have related work outcomes improved, such as time to draft a proposal, error rates or customer response time?
- Can people apply the skills unaided, for example building a useful prompt or checking AI output critically?
For example, after training, a sales team's use of an AI proposal assistant rises from 10% to 70% of deals and proposal preparation time drops by a third.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Certificates on the walls:** displayed certificates show completion at best, not whether anyone uses the skills.
- ✗ **B. Opened the platform once:** a single login measures access, not learning or application.
- ✗ **C. Hours of videos available:** the size of the library measures content supply, not whether employees learned or changed how they work.
- ✓ **D. Applying AI to real tasks with better outcomes (correct):** this shows that skills transferred into daily work and produced business results, which is the program's actual goal.

## Key idea
Judge upskilling by applied use and improved work outcomes, not by logins, content volume or certificates.
Q002390:
## Managing the cut-over from manual to AI
Replacing a working process everywhere at once creates a single point of failure: if the AI underperforms, every region is affected and there is no fallback.
## A lower-risk transition
- **Parallel run**: for a short, defined period, run the AI and the manual process side by side and compare outputs, such as accuracy, turnaround time and exceptions.
- **Phased rollout**: switch one region at a time, starting with one where problems are easiest to handle, and apply lessons to the next.
- **Exit criteria and rollback**: agree in advance what results allow the manual process to be retired, and keep a way to revert if issues appear.
For example, an invoice-processing AI runs alongside clerks for four weeks in one region; once match rates meet the agreed target, that region switches and the next begins.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. All regions on the same day:** a big-bang switch with the manual process retired leaves no fallback, so any defect disrupts operations everywhere.
- ✗ **B. Parallel processes forever:** running both indefinitely doubles effort and cost and never captures the benefits of the change.
- ✓ **C. Brief parallel run, then region by region (correct):** comparing results validates the AI before relying on it, and phasing limits the impact of any problem to one region at a time.
- ✗ **D. Each region decides alone:** without comparing results or a common plan, quality becomes inconsistent and problems go undetected.

## Key idea
Reduce transition risk with a time-boxed parallel run and a phased rollout, not a big-bang switch or a permanent duplicate process.
Q002391:
## Elastic capacity with cost predictability
AI workloads vary: training jobs and seasonal peaks need bursts of compute, while everyday inference may be steady. The cloud lets capacity scale with demand, but finance still wants spending it can plan.
## How to balance both
- **Elastic capacity** scales up for peaks and down afterwards, so you pay mostly for what you use.
- **Commitments** for the steady baseline, such as Savings Plans or Reserved Instances on AWS, lower the price of predictable usage in exchange for a term commitment.
